#8423. Dhaulagiri Summit Push; A Second Skier Appears

The rope-fixing team is heading toward the summit of Dhaulagiri at this moment. We don’t know who else is with them, although judging from his past 8,000m climbs, skier Andrzej Bargiel is likely not far behind.

Makalu Lakpa, the climbing leader of the 14 Peaks Expeditions team, reported he is at Camp 1 today and confirmed the rope fixers are 400m beyond Camp 3 and on their way to the top.

Makalu Lakpa of 14 Peaks Expeditions posted this screenshot of his tracker, locating him at Camp 1 on Dhaulagiri.

Andrzej Bargiel has posted some photos from Base Camp, but the exact date they were taken is not confirmed. Bargiel won’t be the only skier on Dhaulagiri. Spanish mountain guide Borja Real is also intending to climb without supplemental oxygen and ski down to Base Camp. Real has been in Nepal since mid-September, but we just heard of him today, via the Alpymon blog.

Choosing the best high-yield checking accounts may require weeding through some bad ones until you find the one that is a perfect fit.

Everyone should look at the monthly fees, focusing only on those accounts that don’t charge one. Chances are, even with a high APY, you won’t out-earn the monthly fee.

You should also consider what you want out of your account or how you’ll use it.

For example, if you know you’ll be out of the ATM network often, choose a bank that reimburses for non-network ATM fees. Or maybe you want a combined checking and savings account, or prefer a bank that offers robust personal finance tools.

The key is to look at the big picture and ensure you can meet the bank’s requirements including the minimum balance required to waive the monthly fee and earn the highest APY.

Your checking account should work for you, not cost you money, so look closely at what it offers and charges to ensure you choose the best high-yield checking account.

We evaluated dozens of checking accounts to build this list. We considered several key variables along the way. The accounts that made the final cut scored well on most or all variables.

Remember, these are high-yield checking accounts we’re talking about. Yield is a key selling point for the banks marketing them, which is why it’s the most important factor in our analysis.

The best high-yield checking accounts are either truly free, meaning they don’t charge monthly fees. Unfortunately, free checking accounts aren’t as common as they used to be, so we make exceptions for accounts that make it easy to waive monthly fees with a qualifying direct deposit or clearing a reasonable minimum balance.

The best high-yield checking accounts tend to offer sign-up bonuses for new account holders, rewards programs that pay you back for eligible purchases, or both. It’s not a deal-breaker when high-yield checking accounts lack these features, but all else being equal, we prefer that they do.

We believe you shouldn’t have to save up a fortune to benefit from a high-yield checking account. Most accounts on this list have no minimum or very low minimum balances. A few do have maximum balances to earn interest, but those are high enough not to impact most users.

Cash is less and less common these days, but ATM access is still important for many checking account users. And we believe you shouldn’t have to pay a fee to get your money. This is why, all else being equal, we prefer high-yield checking accounts with big, fee-free ATM networks.

Some high-yield checking accounts have geographic restrictions, either because you have to open them in a branch or the banks offering them simply don’t operate in certain states. We exclude accounts with strict geographic restrictions and prefer 50-state coverage when possible.

Choosing a checking account isn’t as simple as it sounds. As you get into it, you’ll almost certainly have some questions, so we’ve preemptively answered some of the most important ones.

It depends on the bank’s policy and prevailing interest rates. However, a good rule of thumb is that the best high-yield checking accounts pay interest on par with the top high-yield savings accounts.

Some high-yield checking accounts attach no strings at all to interest payments, but many do. The most common requirements include:

Many high-yield checking accounts pay interest on all balances, which is ideal if you keep a big financial buffer in your checking account. Others cap interest payments, though. Usually, the cap is relatively high — $5,000 or more.

Ideally, nothing. And the best high-yield checking accounts are indeed free checking accounts. For accounts that charge a monthly maintenance fee, we prefer easy waiver options, such as any direct deposit or a low minimum balance ($500 or below).

Sometimes. The line between checking and savings is blurrier these days because many banks and financial technology apps package checking and savings products into the same digital interface. Several of the accounts on this list are package deals.

Like mortgage rates and CD yields, checking account yields rise and fall as benchmark interest rates change.

During periods of economic uncertainty, when benchmark rates tend to be more volatile, these changes can occur with disorienting frequency. The yield you expect on that shiny new online checking account might not be what you actually receive.

The silver lining is that competition for new checking account customers remains fierce, especially among online banks and smaller brick-and-mortar institutions without household name status.

That means checking account yields will continue to entice new account holders, wherever interest rates go and irrespective of what happens on the savings account front.

#8421. Portugal-to-Singapore Walker Reaches Southern China

German long-distance walker Rainer Mautz left Cabo de São Vicente, Portugal, on February 26, 2025, bound for Singapore. Mautz, who is in his mid-50s, chose his 25,000km route to create the longest possible line across Eurasia. So far, he has covered 18,000km and is now trekking across China.

Mautz set himself strict rules: where possible, every meter should be walked; no interruptions using transport (no journeys home by plane, no using a bicycle to fetch supplies); and he needs to carry his gear, without a cart.

Mautz’s route, including a failed attempt to enter Mongolia. Photo: Rainer Mautz

His route included an extremely unusual stretch. The government permitted him to walk 600km across Turkmenistan over 18 days. “There has never been such a long tourist journey in this country before. According to research by the largest Turkmen travel agency, this set a new record,” Mautz wrote.

Turkmenistan requires government guides to accompany foreigners at all times, and most tourists stop through only briefly, perhaps visiting the Gates of Hell (the Darvaza gas crater, which is still burning decades after it was set alight).

A night with gas pipeline workers in Turkmenistan. Photo: Rainer Mautz

Following the Amu Darya River along the border to Uzbekistan, Mautz walked with a guide named Geldish, followed by a government/tour agency vehicle. In a country so unused to tourists, locals often treated Mautz like a celebrity.

However, the increased attention also caused problems. In the village of Karaaygyr, they were forced to leave in the middle of the night when the owners of the private home they were staying in suddenly got cold feet about having strangers stay. “The villagers didn’t understand what we were doing there,” Mautz explained in his online journal. “When we left the apartment through the living room, it felt like running a gauntlet. Strangers with hostile expressions stood lined up on both sides.”

But curiosity and generosity outweighed fear over the 18 days. “People [repeatedly] handed us gifts from their cars. Each time, we are deeply impressed by how friendly the locals are. Today, we were both given iced tea and money. Resistance was futile; we had to accept 18 manat (about $1.60). After all, those traveling on foot are assumed to be in need. Our refusal was simply interpreted as modesty.”

Mautz’s route has changed a few times, both during the planning phase and on the road. He had planned to cross Mongolia but had to change plans at the last moment. He entered Mongolia in late May 2026 with his wife, Guang. They had walked only six kilometers before arriving at a police checkpoint blocking the road. A foot-and-mouth disease outbreak meant they could not continue.

Rather than wait indefinitely for the situation to improve, the couple chose to return to the border and re-enter China. Mautz then resumed his journey through China, heading southeast.

A scene from Yunnan, China. Photo: Rainer Mautz

He crossed the Gobi and continued to the Yellow River. During August, he crossed the highlands of northern Sichuan, and by September, he was in Yunnan. On September 23, he arrived in the provincial capital, Kunming. During the stretch to Kunming, he made excellent time. Between July 31 and September 23, he took no rest days, averaging nearly 40km per day over 53 consecutive walking days. His total distance now sits at over 18,000km, a little over 70% of his projected route to Singapore.

Though his route remains flexible, he plans to travel through parts of both Vietnam and Laos as he heads farther south to Singapore.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8420. 8 Best Robo-Advisors of November 2026

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Historically, one enormous advantage the wealthy had over the rest of us was access to expert investing advice. They didn’t need to be experts on stocks or market movements or investing. They could pay someone to “just take care of it.”

Today, everyone has access to expert investing advice — if not through human investing advisors, then through robo-advisors.

These are the best robo-advisors on the market right now. Each does one thing really well, whether it’s optimizing tax efficiency without a high balance requirement or keeping management fees in check.

Most of these robo-advisors are appropriate for lower-balance investors just getting started on the road to financial freedom. But most also have features that appeal to more experienced, affluent clients.

Vanguard Digital Advisor is the best overall robo-advisor for U.S. investors right now. Its key selling points include:

Disclaimer—M1 Finance isn’t technically a robo advisor, but its automated investing features stand out and warrant a spot on the list.

M1 Finance allows investors to choose from dozens of prebuilt template portfolios (“expert portfolios”) or custom-build every piece of their portfolio. It’s the best of both worlds: the option to tailor your portfolio without doing the legwork to maintain it, thanks to M1’s dynamic rebalancing.

Wealthfront offers tax-loss harvesting on all accounts, regardless of balance. Most competitors make this feature, which periodically and strategically unwinds losing positions to reduce investors’ taxable gains, available only on higher-balance accounts.

Wealthfront does offer a premium tax optimization feature called Direct Indexing (formerly Stock-Level Tax-Loss Harvesting) on accounts with balances greater than $100,000. Its super-premium Smart Beta feature, available on accounts with balances above $500,000, has even more powerful tax optimization capabilities.

Money Crashers, LLC receives cash compensation from Wealthfront Advisers LLC (“Wealthfront Advisers”) for each new client that applies for a Wealthfront Automated Investing Account through our links. This creates an incentive that results in a material conflict of interest. Money Crashers, LLC is not a Wealthfront Advisers client, and this is a paid endorsement. More information is available via our links to Wealthfront Advisers.

SoFi Invest does not charge a management fee of its own. You’ll still pay fund management fees that can vary depending on the composition of your portfolio, but SoFi won’t take a cut on top of that.

Betterment isn’t the only robo-advisor that offers socially responsible investing (ESG) options, but it does it better than any other. Choose from three Socially Responsible Investing Portfolios:

Ellevest is a robo-advisor platform designed by women, for women. Its proprietary algorithm accounts for the challenges women face in the workforce and the world of finance: pay gaps, extended career breaks, longer life expectancies, and more.

Ellevest adds fee-based one-on-one coaching tailored to the needs of women clients. Top-tier Ellevest Executive plan members ($9/month) get 50% off the hourly rate.

SigFig balances the low cost and hands-off approach of other robo-advisors with on-demand, unlimited access to human financial advisors. It does this at impressively low cost: 0.25% AUM, with your first $10,000 managed free.

Titan Invest is the best robo-advisor platform for serious investors who want to take advantage of advanced, potentially market-beating strategies formerly reserved for hedge funds and professional stock traders.

Titan employs an active asset management posture that has consistently beaten Wealthfront and Betterment. You can choose from any (or all) of Titan’s four award-winning investment strategies: Flagship, Opportunities, Offshore, and Crypto.

We use 8 key metrics to evaluate the robo-advisors on this list. Each factor plays an important role in the account holder’s experience and overall suitability of these products.

Most of the robo-advisors on this list build out investors’ portfolios with ETFs or mutual funds. With few exceptions, these funds charge management fees to cover their own internal costs. These fees are calculated as an annualized percentage of assets invested in the fund.

Most of these fees are relatively low, if only because robo-advisors tend to shun higher-cost, actively managed funds. But even hundredths of a percentage point matter over time, so we’re biased towards robo-advisors whose component funds have very low expenses indeed.

This is the other direct cost you’re likely to encounter as a robo-advisor client. Most robo-advisors charge management fees on top of component funds’ fees.

Like those fund fees, robo-advisor management fees are assessed as an annualized percentage of assets invested. So if your average account balance is $50,000 this year and your robo-advisor charges a 0.25% management fee, your robo-advisor will collect a total of $125 from you over the course of the year.

Many robo-advisors utilize tax-loss harvesting to reduce account holders’ taxable gains. Some limit eligibility for tax-loss harvesting to higher-balance accounts.

Others, like category leader Wealthfront, make this capability available to all. Wealthfront does reserve its most sophisticated tax optimization strategies for accounts with balances above $500,000, however.

Almost all robo-advisors offer general investing accounts (taxable brokerage accounts). Blooom, which exists only to optimize employer-sponsored plan assets, is an important exception.

Some robo-advisors go farther and offer tax-advantaged accounts like IRAs, 529 education savings plans, and custodial accounts (UTMA/UGMA accounts). Many offer joint accounts for couples as well. Our position: The more available account types, the better.

ESG stands for “environmental, social, and governance.” The term “ESG investing” is often used interchangeably with “socially responsible investing” and “socially conscious investing,” even though they technically describe different investing approaches.

Semantics aside, ESG or socially conscious investing options help investors express their values with their dollars. The best robo-advisors for ESG investing, like Betterment, offer multiple socially conscious portfolios that cater to distinct investor priorities: low carbon, workforce diversity, and so on.

Market downturns are a fact of life and no robo-advisor (or financial advisor, for that matter) provides total protection against them.

But some, like M1 Finance, give clients more control over their portfolios’ composition, allowing them to prepare for bear markets as they see fit. And others, like Ellevest, tailor asset allocations and financial guidance to the unique needs of their customers. In Ellevest’s case, that’s professional women.

Robo-advisors are generally beginner-friendly. Some do cater to more sophisticated investors, however. M1 Finance is a good example of a robo-advisor that offers the best of both worlds: easy automation for hands-off beginners alongside near-endless customization potential.

Originally, robo-advisors cut human advisors out of the picture entirely. If you wanted to work with a human financial planner or wealth manager, you had to “upgrade” to a more expensive platform or hire a full-service financial advisor.

These days, the distinction is blurrier. While some robo-advisors remain purist about keeping investors away from human advisors, others have embraced a hybrid model. The best hybrids, like SigFig, do this while managing to keep fees and investment minimums low.

You have questions about robo-advisor apps. We have answers.

A robo-advisor is an automated investing platform that uses complex algorithms to build and periodically rebalance custom or semi-custom portfolios.

Most robo-advisors invest in a mix of index and sector ETFs and mutual funds. While humans build the algorithms and support the system, robo-advisors place trades without direct human input.

Robo-advisors charge two types of fees, one direct and one indirect.

The direct fee is the management fee, which the robo-advisor charges to cover its own expenses. Robo-advisors’ management fees generally come in under full-service human financial advisors’. But they do vary considerably.

Some robo-advisors charge no management fees and offer only limited flexibility. Others offer all the bells and whistles you could ask for — and charge accordingly. They also tend to require a high minimum investment, sometimes in the six figures.

As a general rule, the more flexibility and human interaction a robo-advisor offers, the higher the management fee they charge. Most offer a completely automated option at a lower price point and a human hybrid investing service for a higher cost.

Investors just starting probably don’t need much flexibility. The more wealth you have to invest, the greater your needs and the more flexibility you likely want. You may be willing to pay a higher management fee for better service.

The indirect robo-advisor fee is the sum total of fees charged by any mutual funds or ETFs the investor owns. Robo-advisors can’t directly control these fees, though they do work hard to minimize them.

Most robo-advisors use a mix of ETFs and mutual funds to build their clients’ portfolios. At the very least, they offer clients the option to invest in ETFs and mutual funds, rather than individual stocks. Though robo-advisors seek to invest in high-performing, low-cost funds, fund fees are inevitable.

One area of distinction among robo-advisors lies in the types of accounts they service. Rather than just a taxable brokerage account and IRA account, some robo-advisors service 529 plans, trusts, and 401(k) advising.

Higher-end robo-advisors also offer tax-loss harvesting, allowing investors to adjust their portfolios to reduce their tax bills. That’s a vital feature for higher earners.

Some robo-advisors also offer a socially conscious investing option, which is significant to many investors. Ultimately, your ideal robo-advisor comes down to your priorities and how much you have to invest.

Every robo-advisor gives clients some say over their investments.

Basic robo-advisors typically ask clients a few questions about their long-term goals and tolerance for investing risk, then build semi-customized portfolios based on their answers.

More sophisticated robo-advisors offer the option to invest more purposefully. For example, M1 Finance offers the option to invest in any of dozens of “custom pies,” or mini-portfolios composed of specific securities.

But if you’re really set on picking and choosing the components of your portfolio down to the individual stock level, a robo-advisor might not be the best fit for you at all. A commission-free self-directed brokerage account could be the better choice.

#8419. Uncertain Weather Delays Dhaulagiri Summit Push

It is taking longer than expected for climbers to reach the summit of Dhaulagiri, due to unstable weather and uncertainty about conditions above Camp 3. No one has set foot on those upper sections yet, but a large number of climbers are gathering in Camp 2, waiting for news from the rope fixers.

Today, Paul Clarke of Australia contacted ExplorersWeb from Camp 2. He and his partner, Xenia Santha of Hungary, arrived there on Tuesday and have stayed put, waiting for the right moment to go for the summit. “It seems we will have to wait at least two more days,” Clarke said. “Yesterday, I was able to push up to 6,500m, but then bad weather rolled in.”

The pair hopes to move to Camp 3 tomorrow, deposit some gear, then return to Camp 2. At the moment, they have set the morning of October 12 as a potential summit date.

Paul Clarke and Xenia Santha in their tent at Camp 2. Photo: Paul Clarke/@outdoorpirate

The rope-fixing team stopped just above Camp 3, Clarke noted. “We have been the only ones remaining in Camp 2 for two days, but today, the rest of the team from 8K (three clients) and about five clients from Seven Summit Treks and 14 Peaks arrived, with lots of Sherpas.

Camp 2 on Dhaulagiri as seen from a drone. Photo: Paul Clarke@outdoorpirate

Makalu Lakpa, leader of the 14 Peaks Expedition and Seven Summit Treks teams, has just checked in on social media from “upper” Camp 2. “The rope-fixing team made good progress and…[are] now preparing for the summit push,” he wrote. “The snow conditions remain favorable, and we are closely monitoring the weather.”

Lakpa added that they will start toward the summit “if the weather gives [them] a suitable window,” suggesting that they remain on hold. The exact location of the rope fixers is unclear.

The weather on Dhaulagiri remains uncertain. “Yesterday, we had about 30cm of snow in the late afternoon/evening,” Paul Clarke said. “Today has been overcast and windy…probably around 40kph here in C2.” If it persists, that wind will likely increase higher up the mountain and could thwart any potential summit try.

The Polish skier posted an update from Base Camp yesterday, after an acclimatization trip to 7,000m with Kuba Poburka and Pasang Rinzi Sherpa. “After spending the night at Camp 2, I skied all the way back down to Base Camp,” he wrote. “Now it’s time to rest and wait for the weather.”

Paul Clarke confirmed he saw Bargiel skiing down from Camp 2 on Tuesday, as Clarke worked his way up. It’s unclear whether the skier and his team are still in Base Camp or have gone back up the mountain.

The second skier attempting Dhaulagiri, Borja Real of Spain, has aborted his climb. Real said that conditions on the mountain, especially between Base Camp and Camp 1, and at the traverse above Camp 3, are too dangerous for a ski descent in his chosen style: without supplemental oxygen, no Sherpa support, and carrying his own tent and supplies up and down the mountain.

Borja Real of Spain during a rotation to Camp 2 on Dhaulagiri. Photo: Borja Real

Real said the mountain is overloaded with snow in the upper sections and believes there is no time for it to settle. No one has yet ventured on the long traverse that crosses the upper section of the peak above Camp 3 or the snow couloirs leading to the summit ridge. The 30cm of fresh snow that Paul Clarke confirmed fell yesterday around Camp 2 will likely be an issue in those regions.

Dhaulagiri’s normal route with the three high camps currently pitched, and the final traverse, with the couloir to the summit ridge marked in red. Before supplemental oxygen became common on Dhaulagiri, climbers usually pitched a fourth camp. Photo: Ralf Dujmovits

Real mentioned he didn’t like the way logistics are organized on the mountain these days. He noted that some agencies are offering their clients airlifts to and from Camp 1 as shortcuts to the summit. On Dhaulagiri in the fall, the route from Base Camp to Camp 1 traverses some technical passages with rock sections and open crevasses. Camp 1 sits on the huge Dhaulagiri Col at 5,900m, which provides a suitable place for helicopters to leave and pick up passengers.

The glacier leading to the Dhaulagiri Col where Camp 1 is located, showing the snow-covered crevasses. Photo: Borja Real

#8418. Upgrading To A Home You Don’t Need: A Three-Year Review

Toward the end of 2023, we upgraded to a larger finished home we didn't need. Three years later, I want to share whether it was worth it, so you can make a better decision if you're tempted to do the same.

More than any other material item money can buy, a home is the most desirable. The average person spends over 14 hours a day at home, so there's also probably no investment we use more. Sure, we have to wear clothes in public, but we swap them out every day. And last I checked, my t-shirts and shoes don't appreciate in value.

Fine watches and jewelry are nice and can appreciate too. But we don't wear them every day, and we definitely don't live inside them. So hands down, a home is the best combination of enjoying your money while also potentially making a positive return.

Upgrading to a home you don't need is a slightly different animal.

If you upgrade into something other people find undesirable or unnecessary, your home probably won't give you a positive return you're hoping for. But if you upgrade in the “frenzy zone” price range, the one buyers fight over in your market, you'll almost always have strong demand when it's your turn to sell.

My wife and I talked about this on our podcast, and we've concluded the purchase was worth it.

It took a tremendous amount of convincing to get her to agree to move. She finally acquiesced after I promised this would be our last house ever, assuming we stay in San Francisco. That promise was the main thing that got her over the line.

Our children have enjoyed the extra space tremendously. They play in the enclosed front yard every day, and we don't have to worry about them getting hit by a car or snatched by a stranger. The neighborhood is quiet and safe, although there's now a lot of remodeling going on.

I've also noticed our boy needs to run around more than our daughter, which seems typical. Once he's burned off the energy, it's easier to get him to focus on homework.

If you have a boy, or any extremely active child, a home on a large, usable lot can be beneficial for childhood development. That's something we didn't fully appreciate before buying.

There's also peace in knowing we'll never move again. For 20 years, from 2003 to 2023, I was addicted to real estate and constantly climbing the property ladder. Now that we've reached the top rung we can afford, I feel settled in a way I didn't expect. No more wanting feels amazing!

If you're focused on decumulation, or at least on spending more of the hard-earned money and risky investments that have paid off, it feels good to turn that money into something you actually enjoy.

A nicer home checks the box of being something we use every single day, which is more than I can say for most things I've spent on.

From a purely financial standpoint, the toughest part of upgrading to a home you don't need is thinking about how much more you could have made had you invested elsewhere, usually in stocks.

The S&P 500 is up over 80% since we sold stocks and Treasury bonds to buy our home. The opportunity cost of not making more elsewhere must be weighed against the utility you derived from your home.

It could always be worse, though. I talked to one dad who sold his Salesforce (CRM) stock in 2009 to buy his home. Had he held on, the stock would be up about 10X. I talked to another dad, currently thinking about upgrading, who worked at Tesla and sold shares in 2015 to buy his place. That stock is up more than 20X since.

Both of their properties are also up since purchase. But their old stock positions are up dramatically more.

All in, I'm sure I've left over $1 million on the table by buying our house, net of how much the house has appreciated. The opportunity cost could have been worse, but luckily the San Francisco housing market is strong thanks to AI. It's boom loop time.

I'm not sure we could buy our house today if it came on the market. In 24 years of searching for property in San Francisco, I've never seen a lot this size at this price point. So maybe the market is adjusting higher than I think, especially as the west side of San Francisco gets more popular.

The general recommendation is to set aside 1% of your home's value each year for maintenance. It's a decent rule of thumb, especially if you own a condo with a homeowners association, which I also do.

But after three years in the house, here's what we've actually spent:

That's roughly $4,700 over three years, or about $1,567 a year for pure maintenance. Practically nothing, and far below the 1% rule of thumb.

The low cost isn't entirely luck. We were thorough during the three-month escrow and had the sellers fix as much as possible before closing. The house had also been gut remodeled and fully landscaped right before our purchase, so we bought near the top of its maintenance cycle, not the bottom.

Run through this checklist before you fall in love and experience buyer’s remorse:

1) Make sure your spouse is genuinely on board. Not “fine, whatever” on board. Actually on board and extremely excited. A reluctant partner turns a great house into a recurring argument. Make a promise you can keep, like I did, and mean it.

2) Run the 30/30/3-5 rule. Have at least 30% of the purchase price saved (20% down, 10% buffer), keep the monthly payment under 30% of your gross income, and limit the home price to no more than 3 to 5 times your annual gross income. Break this rule and you invite stress.

3) Buy just above the frenzy zone. Pick a home and neighborhood that buyers fight over, then look for a price point about 10% higher. The frenzy zone is where most people bid, which means bidding wars that can leave you with tremendous buyer’s remorse if you win. Just above it, there’s less competition and better deals.

3) Stress test your cash flow. Model the new mortgage, property taxes, insurance, and maintenance, then assume one income disappears for six months. If the math gives you a panic attack, you’re stretching too far. I went through a six-month period of living paycheck to paycheck which recreated the stress I felt in banking almost every day.

4) Decide mortgage vs. cash with your opportunity cost in mind. Before you sell investments, ask what that money would likely earn if you left it alone, because that’s the cost you’ll feel most. Paying cash removes the monthly payment but concentrates your money in one illiquid asset. A mortgage keeps more invested but costs you fees, paperwork, and a lien.

If you can afford to pay cash and the home is worth 30% or less of your net worth after purchase, the cash route makes sense with interest rates this high. You can often get a better deal, or win the bid, by closing quickly with cash.

5) Hire an inspector and use a long escrow. This is where you create leverage. Find every defect and push the seller to fix as much as possible before closing. Our low maintenance bill is a direct result of being relentless during escrow.

6) Match the home to your family’s actual life. Active kids need a lot to run around on. Aging parents with bad hips prefer a single-story or a guest suite. Buy for how you’ll really live now and in the future, not for the staged photos, and not to impress people who aren’t paying your property tax bill.

In conclusion, we would happily buy this home again. The experience has worked out, but of course, it could easily have not. I cannot get these three years back, but I can appreciate how this house has provided a nicer life for my wife and children.

The one thing I might change is taking out a mortgage so I wouldn't have had to sell so much stock. But a mortgage would have cost about $10,000 in fees upfront, plus more work, plus the bank holding a lien. So maybe not.

Money is meant to be spent and enjoyed while we're still alive. So if you want to upgrade your home, go right ahead. Just follow the 30/30/3-5 rule so you don't put yourself in financial jeopardy and end up too stressed to enjoy the place.

Readers, have you ever upgraded to a home you didn't need? Was it worth it, or do you wish you'd kept the money invested? And if you're on the fence right now, what's holding you back?

Upgrading our home concentrated a big chunk of our net worth in one illiquid asset on one street in one city. Great for the kids. Not great for diversification.

If you want more real estate exposure without selling stocks, fixing fence planks, or paying a plumber at 10pm, take a look at Fundrise. AI may be the next general-purpose technology, but every model needs a physical home. Hyperscalers are pouring hundreds of billions a year into data centers, and power and permitting have become the binding constraint. Real estate is where that constraint gets solved.

Fundrise lets you invest in private real estate passively, with a low minimum. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai, and our investment philosophies are aligned.

My wife and I recorded a podcast episode looking back on our first three years in the house as well, including whether she’s forgiven me for convincing her to move. It's also a great discussion about life after FIRE, parenthood, and tackling growing desires. Listen on Apple or Spotify.

Sign up for the private Financial Samurai newsletter!

Sign up for the private Financial Samurai newsletter!

We recently upgraded our home into my “stretch” zone. We lived in our previous home for 13 years with the intent on keeping it as a rental, +3x the value and low 30 year mortgage

When our new house came up in January this year there was a bidding war and we won. I’m confident it could have gone higher but the seller only wanted to market it for 5 days. We put down 31.5% on the purchase with a 7 year I/O at 5.25%.

I’ve felt a lot of stress when I think of the big picture because I’m somewhat risk adverse. We kept our house with a great tenant for two years that exceeded my rent expectations.

When I get overwhelmed, I step back and take a hot tub (private gate into association pool/hot tub) and look around and realize I’ve upgraded my family to one of the nicest best run beach cities in SoCal. They aren’t making more land, the house brings immense joy to me and my family. We are off the busy street we lived in before and it’s so much more peaceful, safer.

I’ve reached deep into AI to help when I get stressed and it validates the purchase math, my investment thesis, and my belief in the area we invested.

While my business has been down, 100% commission, in the end of the day I realize much of my stress is my mind playing tricks one me by playing out worst case scenarios. The psychology of making life changing big moves is really something else. In a few years, I’ll be more comfortable as I grow into our new reality. Buffet always talks about the psychology of investing and it’s a real doozy.

Yes indeed. The stress of making big investment decisions can really get to you.

In three years, your home should feel much more affordable. Hope you can enjoy it as much as possible.

Better than losing / giving up all your gains in tech stocks this year!

Interesting perspective! Upgrading to a bigger home can be exciting, but the additional costs and long-term financial commitment are important to consider. I think choosing a home based on actual needs and financial comfort is often better than upgrading just for extra space. Thanks for sharing your thoughts!

Sam, Would you watch or update the “30% of your net worth” home purchase rule to reflect home value as it appreciates? Suppose your purchase fits well within that rule at first, but doubles (hey, it could happen) in only a couple years. Now you have significant equity but also very high taxes, insurance, and perhaps even higher maintenance costs. How does that square?

If the home itself surges in value much faster than your overall net worth growth, then it’s just a reason to feel great about your purchase. There’s no need to sell it and buy a new house to get it down to 30% or lower. Enjoy the great purchase and the good times.

The extra cost should be affordable if you bought anywhere near the other two variables.

Regarding the 30/30/3-5 rules, it seems that it’s dependent on income. In other words, a 100K income on 500K home and small down payment vs 500K income with large down payment on 2.5M home looks a lot different. If coming in with a large down payment, that would seemingly impact the 3-5Xs income rule quite a bit vs 3-5Xs the entire purchase price?

Scenarios: 500K income 2.65M purchase price 1.275M down payment 1.375M mortgage

It’s a general guideline to hit within the ranges of the three variables.

The down payment variable is more powerful, where if you put a larger down payment down, you can do a higher multiple of income.

The down payment is more certain, but the income variable can change at any moment.

Figured. Ok, looking to upgrade to a home we don’t need that has quite a few scarcity features that aren’t easy to replicate, so likely a now or never scenario.

It is surprising how fast three years have passed by. We bought a house four years ago with cash, and I am nodding my head in agreement with each of your points. If I had kept the home purchase money invested in Apple, that stock’s value would have doubled. I am reminded of Charlie Munger’s quote, “The first rule of compounding: Never interrupt it unnecessarily.”

Also, the home purchase price pushed up against your “30% or less of net worth” rule.

Neither of these issues have created financial stress in our lives, and we own a very nice house. And, if this home turns into our “forever home” I will also have a “forever job” of fixing things. LOL

That’s great things have worked out. And mainly it’s probably because you spent reasonably, and within my guidelines.

Getting to the point of buying too much house, over five times you’re gross income, and hoping your job will continue to be there and your income will continue to grow is very risky proposition in this market.

What a fun recap and glad to hear it’s worked out well for your family. Any relocation, even if it’s just from one street to the next around the corner, is a big commitment of time, energy, and often higher cost. Any major change is always a risk so that’s great it was worth it for you. There’s also something incredibly priceless about feeling settled and not having to move again. Enjoy your home!

Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway have come to remote western Nepal to look for first ascents in the Karnali and Chandi ranges.

Scouting lines with the help of a drone. Frame of a video from Fredrik Strang’s Instagram

The pair has spent months preparing to climb some virgin 6,000’ers in the area. Strang told ExplorersWeb he’ll report on the expedition after they return. Strang did throw out a hint, however, saying that they passed Saipal Peak (7,031m) on their way to base camp. He has also posted a photo of one of their targeted peaks (no name attached) on social media:

Like many other teams currently in Nepal, they are finding difficult conditions due to deep, soft snow after the recent storms. Still, they summited an unclimbed 5,177m peak on Tuesday. Their main goals will have to wait until conditions improve.

We use several important factors to evaluate small business bank accounts and choose the very best for our readers. As you narrow down your list of suitable accounts, consider each in turn and how it relates to your business needs.

Some bank accounts have more fees than others. Rather than let the perfect be the enemy of the good, we look for small business accounts that keep fees to a minimum. We’re especially sensitive to account maintenance fees. Our ideal business account doesn’t charge those.

Many small business owners, and certainly many microbusiness owners and sole proprietors, can’t afford to keep thousands of dollars in their accounts at all times. All else being equal, we prefer accounts that don’t require large opening deposits or ongoing minimum balances.

Transaction limits are the bane of small business owners’ existence. At least, they used to be. The best small business accounts waive transaction limits altogether, reckoning that an arbitrary cap on inflows and outflows is bad for, well, business.

We don’t hold the lack of interest (yield) on business checking accounts against their backers. But we do give extra weight to banks that find a way to pay interest on eligible deposits, especially when prevailing interest rates remain low by historical standards.

It’s not uncommon to find small business bank accounts offering generous account opening bonuses with relatively few strings attached. Some upstart banks offer referral bonuses and other financial incentives, such as cash-back rewards, as well. We say: the more, the merrier.

Increasingly, great business bank accounts are hubs for actually getting business done, not simply collecting payments and settling bills. We’re big fans of banks that offer a range of features and capabilities, especially third-party integrations with accounting, payroll, and other software platforms. Bonus points for discounts on these services.

These small-business checking accounts aren’t always the stars of the show at their respective online banking institutions.

Most of these banks offer multiple personal and business deposit accounts. Several make our lists of banks with the best CD rates and the best money market rates, and some offer enticing high-yield savings accounts to boot.

So even if you come for the low-cost small-business checking, you could find yourself staying for more. All else being equal, we prefer banks that give you this option.

You have questions about small business banking. We have answers.

However, if you have a business loan or line of credit with your bank, including a business credit card, you can and will build credit for your business. It’s important to use these products responsibly by making timely payments and keeping credit line utilization low. Otherwise, your business credit score could suffer.

Most business bank accounts impose transaction limits and demand hefty minimum balances to waive high monthly maintenance fees (also known as monthly service fees).

That puts microbusiness owners and solopreneurs at a distinct disadvantage. And it’s a stark contrast to the consumer banking world, where the best free consumer checking accounts cater to individuals and joint account holders who aren’t swimming in cash.

Fortunately, friendlier business bank accounts are out there. You’ll find many on this list.

There’s no hard upper limit to the number of bank accounts your business can have.

That said, you shouldn’t open an account just for the sake of opening an account. As your bank accounts multiply, managing them gets more complicated and time-consuming. With many business bank accounts charging maintenance fees and imposing transaction limits, the costs can add up quickly too. So if your business is relatively simple, it probably needs no more than two or three accounts.

If you’ve read this far, you’ve probably noticed that the best small-business checking accounts have certain things in common:

The ideal business checking account for your needs should cover as many of these bases as possible. If you’re not sure where to turn, know that any of the accounts on this list would be a fine addition to your enterprise’s financial portfolio.

#8414. Six Long Walks Across Australia in 2026

A number of long-distance solo walks have been taking place across Australia this year. Some started in 2026, others ended this year. The walkers have all taken different routes. Some are pulling trailers, others wheelbarrows, and one man is doing it dressed in a leopard-print onesie.

Musician Britt Franzmann, known as Birdgirl, spent much of 2026 walking 3,125km from Perth to Melbourne. She started in May, camped along the route, and carried her equipment in a cart. Speaking to SuzieScribbles, she said she has been obsessed with the idea of crossing the country on foot since reading Robyn Davidson’s book, Tracks. She wanted to see what it was like to be in the remote areas of Australia and do something far outside her comfort zone. From the start, she has been very clear about the rules for her expedition: no support vehicles and no shortcuts.

The logistics became one of the defining features of the walk, mainly because Franzmann was pushing her belongings rather than carrying a backpack. Even though this meant she could take more through remote backcountry areas, including (most importantly) her guitar, it also meant that terrain, heat, and the condition of the cart became constant considerations. More than once, the cart fell apart and needed repairs so that she could continue.

The isolation was one of the hardest parts. For huge sections, she had almost no human contact. Franzmann describes herself as an introvert, but she relishes meeting people on the road and having a chat. A huge boost came in mid-June when her dad joined her for a few days. At the same time, it made the loneliness feel more severe when he left.

Along the way, she often focused on reaching the next big town. Two-thirds of the way through, she decided not to do that. She also stopped turning her trek into social media content. After walking for just over four months, Franzmann made it to Melbourne and finished by performing a homecoming concert at the Northcote Social Club.

Mark Gresser completed his 6,023km walk across Australia in 331 days. He started hiking from Steep Point in Western Australia to Cape Byron in New South Wales in July 2025 and reached his endpoint in June 2026. Of the 331 days, 223 were spent walking. His route went via Lambert’s Centre, Australia’s geographical midpoint, and he covered around 35km a day, walking up to eight or nine hours daily. With temperatures reaching 50°C at times, he followed the weather rather than a particular schedule.

Unlike several other journeys in this roundup, Gresser’s expedition was genuinely solo and self-supported. He had no vehicle support, and his route took him through some of the remotest parts of the country, with limited water sources. His solution to the huge distances between settlements was to pull a 1.9m wheeled cart that carried up to 200kg of food, water, clothing, and equipment. Before setting out, he dehydrated hundreds of meals and posted them to resupply points along the route.

He had to modify the route and take a more southerly path when his cart could not make it over the sand dunes of the Simpson Desert. Yet he could not avoid sand entirely. In the Strzelecki Desert, it took him 18 days to cover 463 km, including 120km over dunes. Many were too steep to pull the cart over, forcing him to repeatedly unpack it and shuttle his load in stages.

A view from the tent. Photo: Mark Gresser

Kentaro Jin, who dubs himself the Strange Catman, started his journey in November 2023. Armed with a wheelbarrow of supplies and sporting a leopard-print onesie, he set out from Carnarvon, Western Australia, and started walking toward the Sydney Opera House. Two-and-a-half years and 6,400km later, he made it to Sydney.

He started the journey after breaking up with his girlfriend in Japan. Speaking to We Are Explorers, he said he felt that his “reason for living crumbled in an instant” and so decided to do something he had thought of when he was a student — a long-distance journey.

In 2024, when he had passed 1,000km, Jin told ABC that he was walking for 10 hours every day and sleeping in a tent beside the road during the long stretches between towns. In civilization, he often stayed with locals, making the most of any hospitality offered. One reason his walk took years to complete was that he stopped periodically to rest and work.

The wheelbarrow may seem like an unusual choice, but it was not a gimmick. He was just used to using one. “I felt a sense of destiny with the wheelbarrow. I worked in construction for six years, and the wheelbarrow was a familiar tool,” he commented.

He finally reached the Sydney Opera House on March 14, 2026, but decided to extend the journey. Now he is cycling along Australia’s east coast, pulling the wheelbarrow behind him, and still in his cat-man outfit.

Simon Harvey, also known as Captain Australia, completed his Big Lap of Australia in April of this year. He began from Brisbane in July 2023 and eventually returned to King George Square in his home city after walking over 15,000km around mainland Australia.

He originally estimated that he would walk 30–35km per day, at least six days a week. That meant around 18 months of walking. In reality, the journey stretched across almost three years due to the number of rest periods he needed and the practicalities of life on the road.

Harvey was never going to do this as an unsupported walk, and relied heavily on the network of people he met along the way. Nor was he always solo. On many occasions, he was joined by his wife, friends, and locals he met along the way.  After finishing the walk, he told The Kids’ Cancer Project that he had been given “fresh pairs of boots, hot meals, and countless conversations by people encountered on the road.”

‘Captain Australia.’ Photo: Peri Strathearn

Walking has always been part of Harvey’s life. When he was just 15, he left home and walked from Brisbane to Sydney to live with his grandmother. Years later, having watched his business fall apart during COVID and then battling cancer, he decided it was time to start walking again. “The walk was my vehicle for healing,” he explained.

One Step Max, who has no other public name, is taking a very different approach from everyone else walking across Australia. His journey has no fixed route, no declared finish line, and by his own account, deliberately no plan.

“When I first started this journey, the first rule I made was to make no plans,” he told the Junee Independent. “That way, I can never be disappointed because I never know what’s going to turn up. So, if I need to spend time with somebody, I’ve got time up my sleeve.”

He set off in October 2025 and walked from Albury to Adelaide for two months along the Murray River. He then took a break to avoid the summer heat before starting to walk again.

“I started on the NSW-Queensland border,” Max told the Junee Bulletin. “I went from Goondiwindi to Moree, Bingara, Narrabri and Tamworth, then from Coonabarabran to Forbes, Condobolin, Lake Cargelligo, West Wyalong, back to Forbes, back to West Wyalong, and then Temora.” Now he is walking through Junee.

Max is also the second person in this roundup who decided a wheelbarrow was the best option for toting his kit and supplies. As the warmer seasons approached, he removed 30kg of winter clothing and gear from his wheelbarrow to pare down his load.

The wheelbarrow setup. Photo: One Step Max

His journey is part of a much larger campaign to walk 700,000km, representing the more than 700,000 people estimated to die by suicide globally each year. That would mean walking the equivalent of 18 circuits of the Earth’s equator. According to the Junee Independent, “The suicide awareness advocate has walked almost 155,000 kilometers so far and is now on his fourth lap of the Earth.”

Steve Roberts began his 4,200km walk across Australia on September 14. At first, he considered starting on the east coast at Cape Byron, but as he has no personal connection to that area, he decided to switch the starting point to Coonamble, the town where he was born. His planned route takes him west through Bourke and Broken Hill before crossing the Nullarbor to Perth.

By the end of September, he had walked 350km and reached Bourke. As with the other walkers, meeting locals is an important part of the journey. He regularly chats to people along the route, and has found himself accepting water top-ups, hot showers, and home-cooked meals.

On reaching Bourke, he rested for a few days. The expedition is not about setting speed records. Robert’s father died at the age of 50 — the age he is now. This walk is to prove “that turning 50 isn’t the end of the story.” Roberts has given himself more than 140 days for the 4,200km route, an average of around 30km per day, though this fluctuates depending on the terrain, weather, and how he is feeling on the day. He is now making his way toward Broken Hill.

Unlike other expeditions, this is not an unsupported hike. Apart from many pre-positioned caches of food and water, his family is accompanying him in a support van.

At the end of November, he will take a 10-day break with his family, then resume from where he left off. Regardless of the style of his journey, he has been very clear about one thing — he will walk every one of the 4,200km on foot.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

In statement cycles where you don’t meet the transaction requirement, you’ll earn a token APY only.

Even free checking accounts can have fees if you aren’t careful. Here are the most common fees to consider when opening a checking account:

Consider these pros and cons before assuming a free checking account is the right choice.

We use several important factors to choose the best free checking accounts on the market. Each relates in some way to the overall cost of the account — lower is better — or to its features or overall usability.

It’s less and less common for free checking accounts to require significant opening deposits or ongoing balances.

Minimums are more common in accounts that charge maintenance fees because it’s easier to tie a fee waiver to a particular balance threshold. “Maintain a minimum daily balance of at least $1,500 to waive the $12 monthly maintenance fee” — you get the gist.

Still, you’ll find a few behind-the-times accounts that still require hefty minimum balances. So, all else being equal, we prefer free checking accounts with low or no minimums.

Even as high-minimum checking accounts become less common, rewards checking accounts grow more plentiful. That’s great news for folks seeking a return on their balances, however modest.

We always prioritize high-yield checking accounts over checking accounts with no yields. The best in the business boast yields north of 1%.

Purchase rewards programs aren’t as common in the free checking space as in the credit card world, where cash-back credit cards and travel credit cards seem to grow on trees.

Fortunately, rewards debit cards aren’t absent from the scene. We put a lot of effort into finding free checking accounts that pay users back for everyday purchases — sometimes as much as 5%, 10%, or more on select purchases.

Budgeting with spreadsheets is so 2000s. If you’re comfortable using a mobile banking app, you have an astounding array of choices for budgeting help too.

That’s because some of the best mobile budgeting apps double as banking apps that automatically allocate your income to emergency savings, longer-term goals, and day-to-day expenses. We’re big fans of these two-for-one deals.

At this point, any checking account that’s not mobile-friendly is behind the times. But the best accounts go the extra mile and make it easy — even preferable — to bank on the go. All else being equal, we prefer these accounts and the financial institutions behind them.

When is an online bank more than a bank? When it’s also your brokerage account, home equity lender, education financier, and so on.

We don’t automatically rule out banks that stick to plain-vanilla deposit accounts. We do prefer comprehensive options, though — institutions that make it easy to spend, save, invest, and plan from the same app.

Make no mistake, “free checking” doesn’t mean “100% without fees.” Most of the accounts on this list charge fees for certain types of transactions or activities, such as ATM withdrawals and wire transfers. Fortunately, it’s usually possible to avoid these fees under normal circumstances.

Then again, because “normal” isn’t always a given, the size and type of these fees matter. We look for banks and accounts that keep them to a minimum or waive them entirely.

Still have questions about free checking accounts? Never fear. We have answers.

Not all free checking accounts are totally, 100% free. Depending on which bank you choose, you could encounter some or all of the following free checking account fees:

At many banks, you must pay a monthly maintenance fee to keep your checking account open. Monthly maintenance fees at traditional brick-and-mortar banks can range from a few dollars to $20 or more, depending on the bank and the account’s perks.

To avoid these fees, you may need to maintain a high minimum daily balance, make regular deposits of a certain size or frequency, or execute a minimum number of transactions in a statement period. That’s not always possible if you’re living paycheck to paycheck.

Yes, as long as they have FDIC insurance up to the statutory maximum of $250,000 per account. FDIC insurance protects your checking account balances against bank failures and certain other events that would otherwise wipe them out.

Be aware that FDIC insurance doesn’t protect investment account balances or value stored in alternative assets like cryptocurrencies. If you invest in stocks or crypto with the same app you use for day-to-day money management, those investment balances are subject to more risk.

These days, even “traditional” banks make it easy to open free checking accounts online. In fact, some of the top free checking accounts are “online-only” accounts backed by brick-and-mortar financial institutions.

Use the links on the list above to find your preferred bank’s application page, or visit the website directly and start the online application process. You’ll need to provide basic personal information and funding account information, but the actual application process shouldn’t take more than 10 or 15 minutes.

When choosing from the best free bank accounts, it’s important to take your time and choose wisely. Consider what you need to reach your financial goals and chances are there is an account out there to help.

#8412. Superniño Weather Threatens Aconcagua Season

The Aconcagua climbing season is approaching, but the threat of unstable conditions linked to this year’s superniño is causing headaches for expedition operators, guides, climbers, and rescue teams.

Temperatures on the surface of the Pacific Ocean are so high that the weather phenomenon usually known as El Niño (the boy) has become a superniño for 2026. Warm, wet air from the ocean can result in massive precipitation inland, and for Aconcagua — South America’s highest peak — that means lots of snow.

A graphic illustrating increasing temperatures in the Pacific Ocean.

Argentina’s meteorological service forecasts a colder, more humid spring than usual, both in coastal areas and in Patagonia, the location of Aconcagua. Authorities in Argentina’s mountain province of Mendoza are issuing weather alerts that warn of flooding and intense snow. Several mountain passes are closed and neighboring Chile is also enduring intense rain and snowfall. The webcams at Portillo ski resort, 27km from Aconcagua, show winter-like images.

The effects of the superniño may unfold over several months. It will surely change conditions in mountain areas by the time the Aconcagua season starts in November for trekking groups, and on December 1 for climbing expeditions. Local guiding companies fear that snow-covered trails and flooded rivers may isolate lower camps. Further up the mountain, climbers might have to progress on icy ramps instead of scree slopes, and deal with significant avalanche risk.

Given the circumstances, park authorities will wait before announcing when the season will begin. Local media suggest either December 5 or December 15 as tentative opening dates.

“The [super] niño will reach its maximum intensity in December, when the temperature of the Central Pacific Ocean will be +2.7°C higher than normal,” meteorologists told La Gaceta.

You can see more on the 2026 superniño here:

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8411. Pain And Penalty: Why A Dad Bod Challenge Works When Willpower Doesn’t

If you want to lose weight and gain muscle, join a dad bod or a mom bod challenge. The social pressure to hit your goals will be immense. And if you put a financial penalty for not meeting your goals by a certain date, you will be even more motivated to get fitter.

Since graduating from college in 1999, I've weighed between 164 and 173 pounds at 5'10” tall. I'm currently about 165 pounds, 45 days after the start of my Dad Bod Challenge. The lightest I weighed as an adult was about 153 pounds, which lasted all of one year before I gained the freshman 10+ pounds during college.

After college, my doctor also suggested I should be around 155-157 lbs to hit my ideal weight. So for over 25 years I've been telling myself I'd like to lose 10 pounds. And I've never succeeded, only coming close when I grew to 173 pounds during the first year of fatherhood in 2017, and then again during the first year of COVID. After both periods, I ended up losing about 7 pounds at most.

But after hearing about some fellow dads at my kids' school entering the Dad Bod Challenge and losing a ton of weight while also gaining muscle, I was impressed. This could finally be the impetus I was looking for to lose that stubborn 10 pounds!

Let me explain our setup, so you might be incentivized to create your own. After all, once you're financially on track, you should get physically on track as well.

There are actually 10 of us in the Dad Bod Challenge. Here are the conditions:

$5,000 might sound steep, or to some, it might not sound like much. But overall, the penalty needs to feel painful enough to motivate you to lift weights, exercise, and reduce food consumption. A $1,000 penalty would be enough to get me motivated, while another might need a $50,000 penalty.

$50,000 would be a scary number to lose, especially as cash strapped as I am. However, on the flip side, with such a high penalty, there is no way I wouldn't meet my goals.

Overall, we agreed that $5,000 was a high enough penalty. After about 45 days, the judge also offered dads the option to buy an extension for $500 a week, for up to four weeks. If a dad buys the extension and meets his objectives, he gets all his money back and doesn't have to pay the $5,000 penalty.

This lifeline was a great relief for me given my slower-than-expected progress. But I'm also reluctant to take it because I need PAIN AND PENALTY to keep me motivated.

If you think losing weight is hard, try losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time. Way harder.

Muscle needs protein and calories to grow. A calorie deficit, which is how you lose fat, starves your muscles of the fuel they need. So the two goals fight each other.

Losing weight on its own is relatively simple. Track what you eat and run a daily calorie deficit large enough to hit your fat-loss target by a certain date. You don’t have to do more. You just have to eat less. Exercise helps, but roughly 80% of weight loss comes from diet. And if you exercise too much, you might overeat.

Building lean mass, which is mostly muscle, requires lifting weights. And not casual lifting. You need to lift to failure, where you can’t squeeze out another rep or two. That usually means at least three sets of 8 to 12 reps, adding weight over time to discover what you can really do.

When I was young, piling on more plates was a fun challenge. Now my joints and tendons ache when I push to the max, and that’s when the injury risk spikes.

Fellow dads have torn biceps, triceps, and pecs, and thrown out their backs lifting. My 70-year-old uncle, who looks like He-Man, tore a shoulder muscle this year and needed surgery. He’s out for at least two months.

If I get seriously injured, I will most likely fail the dad bod challenge. To win, or at least not lose, every dad must hit both his fat-loss and lean-mass goals at the final scan concurrently. You can’t hit your muscle target two months in and then lose it during the final 45 days because you focused only on cutting.

Body recomposition is far harder than doing either one alone. And this is my first time doing it

I hadn’t regularly lifted weights in over 10 years before this challenge.

The reasons were mostly laziness and boredom. I also have a shoulder injury that’s nagged me for at least six years. During COVID, I couldn’t throw a softball overhand without pain, so I mostly played first base and occasionally third. I’d rather not have surgery.

My hope was that going from zero to one would produce big gains. But I needed to be careful. If I hurt myself further, I might not be able to lift at all.

For 45 days, I watched what I ate. I cut way back on sugar and carbs and loaded up on protein shakes and chicken. On top of playing tennis and pickleball three times a week for about 1.5 hours a session, I added 30 to 40 minutes of walking a day.

After all that, my DEXA scan showed I’d lost only 2.6 pounds of fat and gained 1.4 pounds of lean tissue. I expected at least 4 pounds of fat loss, so I was disappointed. But I’m pleased with the lean tissue gain.

The good news is I still have about two months to go.

Over the next two months, I need to gain another 1 pound of lean mass and lose 11 pounds of fat. That’s a net loss of 10 pounds, which would put me at about 156.5 pounds. But a DEXA scan can easily fluctuate by half a pound, so my safer target is 156 or less.

I haven’t been under 160 pounds in 26 years, but I’ve dreamed about it, just like how I've dreamt of buying a mansion in paradise. Then reality sets in and bludgeons my hopes into the ground.

Kei Nishikori, a pro tennis player I’ve followed, has played at around 155 pounds at 5'10”. If he can do it, so can I. Of course, he’s a professional athlete who works out five hours a day and I’m a 49-year-old dad who writes. Still, I accepted the challenge.

As a tennis and pickleball player, I want to be lean. Big muscles are nice, but they slow down my speed and hands. It’s one reason you don’t see muscular players on the pro tour. To each their own.

The best part of a Dad Bod Challenge is the group. Everybody is supportive and brings a different nutrition and fitness background. We cheer each other on and answer each other’s questions. Although, some remain completely silent.

I don’t think anybody is primarily motivated by winning the other dads’ money. Everybody seems motivated by the chance to improve their health.

What’s interesting is that the goals aren’t uniform. We entered knowing the penalty and our own targets, but once the challenge started, we could see everyone else’s.

The judges tried to set fair goals and meet each dad where he was. But after seeing all the numbers, I probably should have negotiated a smaller fat-loss target.

For example, my buddy is two inches shorter than me and started 38 pounds heavier. He has to get down to about 196 pounds while I have to get down to 156 pounds. Our body compositions are different, as he has more lean mass, but losing a similar percentage of fat when you have less of it is harder.

That's life. Which brings me to the lessons a Dad Bod Challenge teaches about money and life.

Getting ripped and wealthy doesn't just happen. You've got to make it happen. Nobody is coming to save you.

The only reason I exercise is because tennis, pickleball, and softball are fun. If they weren’t, I wouldn’t. I don’t run for fun. I don’t walk for fun, although I do enjoy a nice hike.

This lack of fun is the main reason I stopped lifting weights. If I’m going to lift something heavy, I want to be productive, like hauling rocks and bags of mulch for a landscaping project. Curling a dumbbell in a gym felt pointless.

A Dad Bod Challenge forces discipline when fun isn’t enough. It gets you out the door for a 6 am run before work, or to the gym at 9 pm once the kids are in bed. The challenge also helps you get used to that throbbing feeling of hunger, which may make you more appreciative of the things you have.

Make the challenge long enough, 100 to 180 days, and the discipline compounds until it becomes part of your weekly routine.

Building wealth requires the same consistency. You need the discipline to save as much of each paycheck as possible, and the courage to put those savings at risk. Historically, stocks have gone up in roughly 70% of years. That’s when you feel great about your efforts, like losing fat and gaining muscle. The other 30% of the time, you lose a little or a lot and curse your timing, like getting injured.

Stick with both routines for 10 years and you’ll be blown away by the results. But staying disciplined for that long is hard. That’s where a workout buddy more gung-ho than you helps. It’s also where an automatic 401(k) contribution from every paycheck and an AI investment advisor helps.

Some people are born to wealthy, loving parents. Others are born into poverty, given up for adoption, or lose their parents as babies. Some people befriend the founders of a hot AI company and join before it hits it big. Others join startup after startup that goes bust.

The body is similar. Some people are born with fast metabolisms and uncanny strength. Others pack on weight despite working out constantly. Tall, skinny people may struggle to add muscle. Shorter, stockier people may bulk up with ease.

At 49, I'm one of the oldest dads in the group. The youngest is 39. Ah, I remember 39. I was five years into FIRE, traveling the world, and recovering much faster than I do now. I also didn’t have my shoulder and knee injuries. But the challenge gives older dads no handicap. No easier fat-loss targets, no lower lean-mass goals, no extra free time.

Compare your goals to someone else’s and you might get annoyed, because you have completely different genetics. The judges try to set fair goals, but they won’t get it perfect every time.

We can’t control the hand we’re dealt. We can only control our effort and attitude. So compare your progress to your old self and nobody else. If you hit your own goals, you won’t lose. If you happen to win some money too, great. The money was never the point.

What I love about my Dad Bod Challenge is that the creators and judges are fitness fanatics. They’re smart, enthusiastic, kind, and extremely fit. They’ve experienced the benefits of being in shape, so they’re paying it forward by organizing a challenge for 10 dads who are nowhere near as fit.

I’ve learned a ton about how to train, what to eat, how to recover, and how to supplement with protein. One example: spread your protein out, eating about 20 to 25 grams every few hours instead of cramming it all into one meal for better utilization.

Oh, and did you know a tablespoon of olive oil is around 120-140 calories?! Nuts!

I also lost all my excuses. I used to tell myself only people without kids or demanding jobs could get extremely fit. But the judges are dads and successful entrepreneurs. Excuses gone.

Paying it forward is also why I’ve published three times a week on Financial Samurai for over 17 years. No courses, no paywalls, just free content based on my experiences to help you reach financial freedom sooner. When I find a great strategy, like negotiating a severance if you plan on quitting anyway, I find it impossible not to share it.

Before this challenge, I had never measured my lean mass. I just stepped on a scale. But a scale lies by omission. You could lose two pounds of muscle and think you’re making progress. That's no good, especially for folks over 40 who begin to lose muscle more rapidly.

The DEXA scan showed me the truth. After 45 days, I’d lost 2.6 pounds of fat and gained 1.4 pounds of lean body mass. The scale only showed a 1.2-pound difference, which would have been demoralizing. The DEXA showed real recomposition, but also still a bummer because I thought I would have made greater gains.

Finances work the same way. Plenty of people only look at their income or checking account balance and think they’re doing fine. But income is just the scale. Net worth is the DEXA scan. It shows whether you’re building assets or just shuffling money around while debt quietly piles up.

I’ve tracked my net worth since 1999 and it’s one of the best financial habits I’ve ever built. Whatever you measure regularly, you naturally start to improve.

Empower is what I use to track my net worth once I moved on from spreadsheets in 2012. Mezzi is what I use to track my public investments and gain powerful financial insights to better optimize my portfolio.

At the end of the day, I want to build muscle and lose fat to increase my chances of living a longer, healthier life.

That’s primarily why I think more people should join a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge. Even if you miss your exact targets, you’ll likely finish in better shape than when you started.

In high school and college, I stayed in shape to have the widest dating pool possible. My four years at William & Mary were a blast.

Once I started working, good dieting and regular exercise went out the window. During my first five years, staying under 170 pounds was a struggle. Eventually I settled into the mid-160s, playing competitive USTA tennis for 10 years and wanting every edge I could get.

Now, I want as much energy as possible to play with my kids. And I want to live long enough to meet my grandchildren.

So if you need a reason to get in shape and change your body composition, organize a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge. Even if you lose, you’ll probably make new friends and end up fitter.

Here’s to greater strength and 156 pounds or less by December 23, 2026. More importantly, here’s to a lifetime of healthier habits going forward.

Readers, have you ever joined a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge with real money on the line? How big does a financial penalty need to be before it actually changes your behavior, $500, $5,000, or $50,000?

Life insurers notice when you get in shape. Your weight and health history help determine your health class, which drives your premiums. I had my first child two months before turning 40, so my kids will depend on me well into my 60s. Term life insurance is the cheapest way to make sure they’re OK if I don’t make it to grandparent duty.

If you have dependents, check out Policygenius. You can compare quotes from multiple top insurers in one place instead of calling around. The best time to lock in a policy is while you’re young and healthy. The second best time is right after you finish a Dad Bod Challenge. Both my wife and I got matching 20-year term life insurance policies with Policygenius and we feel mentally great as a result.

Sign up for the private Financial Samurai newsletter!
