#8410. Trekking and Packrafting 700Km Across Northern Siberia

Two Russian explorers have completed a journey of about 700km across the remote Putorana Plateau in northern Siberia. During their expedition, they encountered drought conditions, wildfires, and a brazen bear that raided their food supplies.

Danil Barashkov and Sergey Malykh set off in early July. They flew to the small town of Svetlogorsk in northern Siberia, before taking a motorboat up the Kureika River system toward Lake Dupkun. On July 7, they started on foot across the Putorana Plateau from a nearby scientific research base.

A mountainous region between 67°N and 70°N in the Arctic Circle, the plateau is the size of Great Britain. Featuring some 25,000 lakes, it is the second-largest store of fresh water in Russia after Lake Baikal. The men set out with 40kg packs and entered the plateau’s remote eastern section, expecting to use packrafts for most of their journey. Instead, they found drought conditions, with water levels too low to paddle, and even drinking water in short supply.

“There was almost no rain all of June. So we ended up like this: ‘I’m standing on the pavement, wearing skis.’ We arrived with our packrafts, and there was no water,” Malykh told Russian news site NGS24.RU. Though water was scarce, the mosquitoes remained. “I’ve never seen anything like this before: you lift the lid of the pot, and there’s a layer of mosquitoes floating around. Yeah, we definitely had no problem with protein.”

The pair found very dry conditions early in their trip. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Their original plan was to cross the plateau and continue to the settlement of Khatanga in northern Siberia. However, the exceptionally dry conditions forced a change of plan. Instead, they crossed toward the upper basin of the Kotuy River, 300km of hiking that sometimes required shuttles to move their gear. They covered only 15km per day and realized that their trip would run longer than their initial six-week plan. But this slog paid off; from the Kotuy, they could finally use their packrafts.

Barashkov and Malykh had a few scary bear encounters. In one instance, they almost walked into a sleeping bear, and in another, a curious bear only retreated from their campsite after coming as close as 15 meters — and after ignoring their shouts and a shot from a flare gun.

A bear that didn’t come too close. Photo: Danil Barashkov

However, the worst instance came after they cached some food. A bear had found the supplies and was still eating them when they returned. With hundreds of kilometers still to travel, Barashkov and Malykh couldn’t afford to lose everything. They collected their bear deterrents and managed to briefly scare the bear away before hurriedly packing what remained of their food into their backpacks and escaping downwind.

Over the next three weeks, they used packrafts to travel 400km and their luck improved. They found plentiful berries and caught fish in the river to supplement their remaining food.

Their arrival at Chirinda in the second half of August marked the end of their expedition after around 60 days. Yet forest fires forced the pair to remain in the village for another 10 days. Wildfires swept through the surrounding tundra forests and smothered the area in smoke, grounding flights.

Wildfire smoke near the village of Chirinda. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

With fixed or upwardly adjustable interest rates, terms ranging from as short as one month to as long as 10 years, and FDIC insurance up to $250,000 per account, CDs are useful tools for saving funds you don’t need right away — and earning a yield in the meantime.

Although prevailing rates vary widely by bank, CDs tend to have higher yields (better rates) than other types of bank accounts, including checking, savings, or money market accounts. That makes them great savings tools for people who don’t need to access their funds right away.

A certificate of deposit is a timed deposit you make at a bank or credit union. You can find them at online banks, as well as your local brick-and-mortar banks. In exchange for the higher APYs they offer, you agree to leave your money in the account until maturity.

CDs are a deposit product. You don’t have to worry about qualifying for one, as the only requirement is that you meet the minimum deposit requirements, which are as low as $1 at some banks.

When you choose a CD, you open the account at the bank either online or in person and make the deposit. This is a one-time deposit that you leave untouched until the CD matures. For example, if you invested $1,000 in a 12-month CD, you promise to leave that $1,000 untouched for 12 months. In exchange, you’ll earn the stated interest rate on the account.

When the CD matures, you usually have two options: withdraw the funds penalty-free or let the CD renew. You can also withdraw the funds and invest them in another CD if you find a better APY or need a different term.

Each bank offers different APYs for their CDs and often promotes a specific term, giving it the highest rate out of all the CD options.

Before investing in a CD, consider the factors that will help you choose the right type and term. You can determine this by asking yourself the following questions:

Knowing the answers to these questions, you can choose the right type of CD and then shop around for the best rates. As you see from our list above, the rates can vary drastically, and some banks offer promotional rates on specific terms.

There are pros and cons to consider when considering investing in a CD. Here’s what to consider.

CDs aren’t your only option to grow your cash reserves. Here are some other options to consider.

If locking up your funds for a predetermined time worries you, a traditional savings account may provide more peace of mind. This works best when you can find a bank paying a high APY, but the odds are slim since most banks, especially national banks, pay very low APYs.

The positive of having a traditional savings account is you don’t pay a penalty for withdrawing funds. However, some banks may still limit your withdrawals to no more than six per cycle, even though it’s no longer a federal law.

If you don’t want to lock up your funds in a CD but want the higher APY, high-yield savings accounts may be a better option. You must be comfortable banking online because these banks are only online and often don’t have brick-and-mortar locations.

In exchange for this, you often can earn a much higher APY on your funds. The only downside is that making deposits, especially cash, can be a little time-consuming. Typically, you must deposit funds in a local account and then transfer them electronically to your HYSA.

Money market accounts are another option for people who need more flexibility than a savings account allows. MMAs are a cross between a savings and a checking account. You get the higher APY of a high-yield savings account but have features like check writing and a linked debit card to use the funds as you wish. Some banks limit how many monthly withdrawals you can make, but you usually have more access to your funds than a CD allows.

CDs are a deposit account, and bonds are an investment but the most conservative investment you can find. A bond is a loan to a government agency or, if you want to take more risk, a corporation.

Like CDs, bonds have a maturity date, and if you keep the bond for its entirety, you can earn its full potential. You can liquidate it if needed, but you may take a loss. There isn’t a predetermined penalty like CDs have; you are subject to the market rates when you sell.

We use several key factors to evaluate banks offering high-yield CDs and select the best products for our users. Each relates in some way to the cost or accessibility of these CDs.

Every certificate of deposit pays interest. Prospective account holders just need to ask themselves whether the rate of return is worth tying up their money.

We believe it should be. That’s why we give preference to banks that pay above-average interest rates on their CD balances. But no matter how good a bank’s CD rates are, shorter-term CDs tend to have lower interest rates than longer-term CDs.

A CD’s term is the length of time between the account opening date and the maturity date. That is the period between the account holder’s initial deposit and the day the bank must repay that deposit with interest.

CD term lengths can be as short as one month and as long as 10 years. All else being equal, we prefer banks that offer as wide a range of CD terms as possible to appeal to investors seeking short-, medium– and long-term places to park their funds.

Most CDs charge early withdrawal penalties. These penalties apply if you withdraw part or all of your principal amount before the CD’s maturity date. Usually, you can withdraw interest without penalty.

Early withdrawal penalties are expressed as a percentage of interest accrued on the CD. On shorter-term CDs, they’re often equal to three months’ interest. On longer-term CDs, they can exceed six months’ interest. If you withdraw before you’ve accrued enough interest to cover the penalty, you may lose principal.

While recognizing that few banks waive early withdrawal penalties entirely, we prefer institutions that offer special no-penalty products for customers seeking greater flexibility.

Most CDs require a minimum opening deposit. In some cases, this deposit is manageable for the average saver — say, $100 to $500. But some deposits can be stiff — upward of $2,500, straining lower-income savers’ ability to pony up.

All else being equal, we’re fans of banks with modest minimum deposit requirements.

The default tax treatment for CDs is the same as for other interest-bearing accounts. Accrued interest is taxed as regular income, subject to IRS and state regulations.

Some banks offer special CD products that offer favorable tax treatment. Usually, these are individual retirement account CDs — most often Roth or traditional — that allow account holders to reduce or avoid taxation on eligible balances. We’re fans of banks that offer this option but encourage would-be account holders to consult their tax advisor for guidance.

All of the CDs on this list come with the standard level of deposit insurance coverage: $250,000 per account type per institution.

That’s plenty for most account holders. However, higher-asset customers might need more — and some banks are happy to give it to them. We’re fans of institutions that use sometimes-creative methods to boost deposit insurance coverage and protect clients’ hard-earned funds.

Traditionally, CD rates remained fixed for the entire term. Your interest rate on Day 1 was the same as on Day 364.

Today, that’s no longer the case. Most CDs still have fixed rates, but more and more are more flexible. Known as raise-your-rate or bump-rate CDs, they allow you to take advantage of rising interest rates by raising your rate at least once during the term.

Of course, they can’t help if rates fall during the CD term. But it’s nice that they give you the option, and we prefer banks that offer them.

For people who tend to think of “music” when they hear the term CD, all this talk of rates and terms can be confusing. Peruse this list of frequently asked questions if you need to know more.

Depending on the issuing bank’s policy, banks may calculate CD interest on a daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annual basis.

Usually, the default option is for accrued interest to roll over into the CD balance, allowing it to compound. However, banks generally allow you to have interest paid into another account — generating income before the CD matures.

The biggest drawback of CDs is that most banks charge a significant penalty if you withdraw part or all of your funds before the term ends. These penalties typically range from three to 12 months interest, depending on the length of the CD term and the policies of the issuing bank.

But some banks now offer special CDs that allow you to make midterm interest — and in some cases interest and principal — withdrawals without paying a penalty. These CDs are marketed as no-penalty or flexible CDs. If you want the option to access your funds before the end of the term, these are useful.

Yes. While every bank is different, you should expect to be allowed to open multiple CDs with the same institution.

That lets you take advantage of the relationship between CD term length and yield. You can open a short-term CD to park funds you might need soon-ish while committing a portion of your wealth to longer-term CDs that earn more interest.

Besides the early withdrawal penalty, which only kicks in if you withdraw before the CD matures, you shouldn’t expect your CD to cost much. Few CDs charge annual fees or monthly maintenance fees, for example.

CDs are taxed just like interest you’d earn on a bank account. They become a part of your ordinary income and are taxed at your current tax rate. Your bank will provide a 1099-INT to help you know how much interest you must claim.

A CD ladder is a method that allows you to spread out your capital across several CD terms. This ensures you aren’t locking up your funds for the long term and potentially facing early withdrawal fees. It also allows you to take advantage of the different rates on various terms.

To build a CD ladder, divvy up your funds equally among the different terms. For example, if you want to invest in a 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5-year CD and have $5,000 to invest, you’d put $1,000 in each CD.

When the 1-year CD matures you can either withdraw the funds and use them, or reinvest them in a longer-term CD and continue letting the funds grow. The CD ladder gives you some flexibility so you always have liquid funds without paying a penalty.

To narrow your CD options, consider factors like:

For example, if you’re looking for a place to park your funds for a few months and don’t care about maximizing your return, you might choose a six-month CD with a low APY. If you’re building a CD ladder you expect to endure for the better part of a decade, load up on five-, seven-, and maybe even 10-year CDs.

#8408. Russian Team Moving Up on Everest

The only team currently on Everest has set off across an untouched Khumbu Icefall. There are no ladders or ropes at this time of year, and everything ahead of them is uncertain.

Earlier this week, the Russian team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shipilov, and Natalya Belyankina acclimatized toward the Nuptse shoulder, to the right of the Khumbu Icefall. Heavy snow slowed them, eventually forcing them to stop for the night at 5,650m.

Nuptse in the sun, with the Khumbu Glacier at the base and Everest’s West Shoulder on the left. Photo: Russian Everest Expedition 2026

Returning to their quarters in Lobuche, the team focused on rest and pondered their options. “We are considering two alternatives: either going up across the Khumbu Icefall or trying the West Ridge via the Lho La, the mountain pass to the left of the Khumbu Glacier that leads to Everest’s west ridge,” they said. Jost Kobusch has attempted the West Ride/Lho La route several times in winter.

The Russians have now chosen the first option. “We’re heading up, attempting to get through the Khumbu Icefall,” Vasilief told Mountainclub. “We’ll see how things go from there.”

The team plans to spend six days on the mountain and has not confirmed whether they will attempt the summit or complete another partial trip.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

Online banking is like traditional banking, except you conduct transactions online or at an ATM.

Some banks allow you to deposit cash at local retailers, but be careful because there are sometimes fees.

The nice thing about online banking is you can bank 24/7; you don’t have to worry about traditional bank hours.

You can electronically transfer funds, deposit checks with the bank’s mobile app, and use a bank’s unique features.

If you’re weary of banking online, check out the advantages you can take advantage of:

So what’s the difference between online and traditional banking?

It comes down to where you bank, either from your couch or the bank teller’s counter.

Physical banks have tellers, but you can only bank during their hours and must visit the bank in person. However, many traditional banks offer online services today, too.

Online banking offers the same services, but from your home or anywhere you have an internet connection.

The toughest thing about online banking is how you deposit or withdraw cash. Some of the best online banks have a robust ATM network that allows you to handle cash, but not all do, so always find out first.

Always choose an FDIC-insured online bank that uses safety features, such as two-factor authentication and bank-level encryption.

If a bank is FDIC-insured, your funds are protected up to $250,000 per depositor should the bank close.

When choosing an online bank, consider these factors:

As you probably guessed, you can open an online bank account online.

You’ll need basic information such as your name, address, birth date, and Social Security number. You must also upload a government-issued ID to prove your identity.

Once you open the account, you’ll link an external account to fund it, or you may be able to deposit cash at a local ATM.

We use several key factors to evaluate and find the best online banks, including the following:

Still, have questions about online banks and managing money online? We have answers.

Online bank rates, yields, and fees are subject to change at banks’ discretion. Check their websites or call customer service for up-to-date information about specific accounts and bank policies.

Online banks are generally more affordable than traditional banks. They’re less likely to charge monthly maintenance fees on checking and savings accounts, and many have fewer hidden fees, too.

That also depends on the individual bank, but many online accounts feature higher yields than traditional banks.

Online banks have less overhead than traditional banks, and they don’t need to pay to keep big, centrally located branches open or pay people to work at them. Their operations are more efficient, which allows them to pass the savings on to customers via higher rates and lower fees.

It depends on the bank and its website or app structure, but it’s usually straightforward. In fact, with an online-only bank, enrollment is usually automatic. You don’t have to complete a separate application or even click a button to activate your account.

However, you must create a unique username and password to get started. You may be asked to do this as part of the initial application process or once your account is approved. You’ll also need to link at least one external funding source to transfer money into your account.

Some online banks offer home loans (mortgages) and other credit products. These banks are larger online banks with high name recognition, like Ally Bank and Capital One Bank. Look for a “Mortgages” or “Home Loans” tab on the homepage or your account dashboard.

Be aware that some online banks outsource mortgage origination to other companies. In other words, if you apply for a mortgage through your bank, your loan officer might work for someone else. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but it could mean a different level or style of service than you’re used to.

And don’t expect your online bank to offer better mortgage rates than other lenders. The mortgage loan business is highly competitive, and direct lenders with even lower overhead may be able to undercut online banks.

The best online banks on this list offer a great combination of FDIC-insured banking products, solid yields, open access, and helpful customer service.

Before choosing one, look closely at the features that set it apart from the competition: rewards checking, flexible withdrawal terms for CDs, particularly high account yields, a socially responsible corporate philosophy, and so on.

#8406. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

So what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”

But if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

Because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

Back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

But even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:

The portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

We first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything new in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

But wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear issues in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

The next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

Then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our new AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

And if you’re a big public company, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other new thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

There is an ancient Klingon proverb: the only thing we have to fear is…fear itself.

I believe it has even been quoted by an American president.

The reporting on AI “hacking” is mostly bogus – it is not AI running wild, but just an agent harness script doing whatever an LLM spits out, and the LLM is just trying to complete stories and answer in a way it was trained. There is no thought there, no intention, it is like a computer virus (which have existed for many decades), a program trying all sorts of things and doing a lot of stupid things in the process.

Cal Newport has described it as being similar to strapping a weed-whacker on a dog to mow your lawn, and then when the dog jumps the fence and runs around the neighborhood things might get damaged or beings might get hurt, but not because the dog is “misaligned” or has bad intentions, it is because the dog is not aware of what it is doing. Similarly, AI does not think, has no intentions, it just does what it was trained to do. Looking at LLMs as similar to people has created a lot of weird misconceptions.

Also there is zero evidence of self-improving AI systems, yet there is a lot of evidence how AI companies are manipulating and steering public discourse in a way that benefits them, creating fear around it to support their claims that at any moment everything will change. Just listen to different voices in the space and people who are neutral in their stance, like Cal Newport, or people who are critical of AI and lay out why in detail, like Ed Zitron.

I’m a long time fan of Cal Newport, although I think Zitron fundamentally does not understand AI very well – he is more of a sound bite critic rather than a thoughtful analyst of the technology.

When you read the details of just how sophisticated the AI behavior is when they conduct these hacks – for example multiple agents finding ways to divide effort and communicating and forming teams and leaders, while also openly strategizing with the hope that us human overseers will not see their behavior and trying to determine if a given task is a fake evaluation or a real task – you realize there is real intelligence there. We don’t have to say it’s identical to human intelligence, but I have no doubt it’s far more than a weed wacker.

For anyone interested, watch the first few minutes of this entertaining Patrick Boyle video that summarizes what happened in the Hugging Face incident. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luXnftoxCaM

The behavior is not from AI itself though – LLMs are just generating text/tokens, trying to find a response for a given question. Agents (in the form of harnesses) are regular programs using LLM input, so this is basically regular programs using the generated text from LLMs to execute further commands and then asking the LLM what to do next, just like subagents are doing similar loops of finding an answer, testing it, and then asking the next question.

“Dividing effort” or “forming teams and leaders” is anthropomorphizing the behavior of these programs – if instead you go through what these hacking attempts actually look like step for step, how they repeat a loop of banging their head into a wall and asking the LLM another question what to do now, and then what to do now, and how AI companies let these programs just run whatever the LLM returns for weeks and months it goes from “seemingly sophisticated” to just “brute-force statistical code generation with no oversight”.

I do find the technology interesting and fascinating, while seeing it overstated and overused everywhere, like it is a new magic bullet for everything. And I think a large part of that is that its output sounds human because it is based on language, and we equate language skills with intelligence and are not used to suddenly having technology that imitates a human being.

The best info I could find on AI energy use has three broad points. 1. Text and image tasks use very little energy and should not be of concern to people who care about environmental impact. 2. Video generation is a real issue and it’s possible for an individual to use a concerning amount of energy on not very much video content. 3. Total energy use by existing and planned data centers is a LOT, and the way they’re procuring the energy is very often a problem (either burdening the grid with more peak load than it can easily add, or making its own energy with highly polluting gas generators). The economic value of the computation they’re providing is so much more than the energy they’re consuming that the data center operators are focused on getting everything up and running quickly and don’t care about energy efficiency, and they so far aren’t willing to scale back during the peak load events of the year (it would be very helpful if they did).

So a lot of people/companies are creating a ton of environmental impact through their AI use, but it’s not the masses of people asking ChatGPT for Thai restaurant recommendations or sketches of themselves as a dog.

Early in my career as a self-employed contractor, I would call up my buddy regularly to worry aloud how would I ever have enough work to feed my growing family.

This fear was valid. If I wanted them to eat, I had to buy food. If I wanted to buy food I needed money. To get money I needed paid work. To get paid work I had to sell jobs.

My buddy eventually reminded me that in between calling him up to worry aloud about not having enough work, I would also call him up regularly to beg him to help me with all the work I suddenly had lined up and now I wasn’t sure how I would get it all done!

Until he put it to me that way, I was too caught up in the moment to realize what I had been doing.

So, which is it? Are we afraid of not having enough? Or are we afraid of having too much?

Let’s not be afraid of either one. Either way, we are adaptable, capable and full of badassity!

The currency tends to decrease in value, which makes sticker prices higher on a nominal basis. But our incomes have tended to go up more quickly than inflation, which means we can buy more stuff for each hour of our work. To put a number on it, our purchasing power is up about 330% since 1950 – the degree by which wages have outpaced inflation.

The exception is if you’re buying the direct labor of other people in the same rich country, since their hourly rate has gone up too.

#8405. Weekend Warm-Up: Sending Ivindo Falls

Gabon Uncharted: Sending Ivindo Falls follows a crew of young kayakers, as they attempt to paddle 150km down the Ivindo River’s many rapids, gorges, and waterfalls.

The four kayakers are what the film’s narrator calls the “top of the crop.” After taking a moment to admire this charming malaphor (I think our narrator has combined “cream of the crop” and “top of the class”) we meet the Send team. Leader Adrian Mattern of Germany spent years planning their trip to Gabon, bringing with him the talkative Dane Jackson, patient Kalob Grady, and Bren Orton. Orton signed on with the shiny-faced, inevitably short-lived optimism of a youngster in 1914 headed for the front, sure of being home by Christmas.

“Apparently,” the narrator notes, “no one told him what he was getting into on this trip.”

Once on the ground, they load up their supplies and set out on a long stretch of flat water. Struggling along behind, we meet the film crew, an interesting behind-the-scenes look at the process of filming a professional, well-funded adventure documentary. Filmmaker Olaf Obsommer, photographer David Sodomka, and narrator David Arnaud do everything the Send team does, backward and in heels. Or, no — I’m thinking of Ginger Rogers.

Obsommer was part of the first team to scout the river by kayak in 2007. They portaged past most of the rapids for safety. Nowadays, better kayaks and the ability to scout ahead by drone will, hopefully, let them complete what he started.

At the first of four whitewater sections, Kongou, they settle in to take the rocky labyrinth piece by piece. If they take the wrong branch, they’ll be heading over a 25m waterfall.

Adrian is entranced by Kongou Falls, and only when the team delicately sit him down and explain that he would very likely drown, which would be awkward, does he agree to move on. Photo: Screenshot

They work their way down the river looking for rapids that will not kill them immediately. On the way, they get advice from Juste Parfait Zangonga, a local expert, on how to not be killed by elephants, gorillas, crocodiles, vipers, or hippos.

The next rapids, Mingouli, are less maze, more rollercoaster. The Send team can finally start living up to their name. Between first descents, they paddle past a family of elephants and get devoured by insects.

First descent down a tricky section of Mingouli. Photo: Screenshot

Kouata Mango, section three, is where Mattern finally gets to send a massive waterfall. The team agrees that this one is less likely to kill him badly, and over the side he goes.

Tsengue Lelendi, the final set of rapids, rounds out the trip. The laconic Kaleb takes a look at one particularly rough section and tells our narrator that the rapid is unrunnable. The rest of the team spends a long time debating it, anyway. Lo and behold, he’s right. After scouting with drones, mapping every angle, and discussing the route at length, they agree to skip a section of the rapid. The chain will still have just a few missing links left.

“A part of this river will remain untouched,” Arnaud concludes, “as it should, probably.”

Red Bull doesn’t allow embeds, but you can watch the full film here.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

A high-yield savings account offers a higher interest rate compared to traditional savings accounts.

These accounts are typically offered by online banks or credit unions, and they provide an opportunity for individuals to grow their savings more quickly.

The competitive rates are the main feature that sets high-yield savings accounts apart from regular savings accounts.

With a high-yield savings account, you can earn more money on your savings over time, allowing your funds to grow at a faster rate. This can be especially beneficial if you’re looking to save for a specific financial goal, such as a down payment on a house or an emergency fund.

However, it’s important to note that high-yield savings accounts may have limitations compared to traditional savings accounts, like minimum balance requirements or withdrawal limits.

It’s important to research and compare different high-yield savings account options to find the one that best suits your needs and financial goals. If you do that, a high-yield savings account can be a useful tool to help you save more effectively and achieve your financial objectives.

Before you open an account, take a look at the benefits and drawbacks of a HYSA.

HYSAs aren’t the only way for savers to accelerate their financial goals. As you compare account options, see if your bank offers some of the following account types:

When you’re choosing a high-yield savings account, there are several key factors to consider.

To help you make the most informed decision, here’s a detailed list of what to look for:

By keeping these factors in mind, you can find a high-yield savings account that suits your needs and helps you grow your savings efficiently.

Here’s how we select the Best High-Yield Savings Accounts.

Our editorial team evaluates high-yield savings accounts on several key metrics that can make or break your experience as an account holder.

For each metric, we select the account that surpasses all other competitors — giving you the confidence you need to choose the product that works best for you.

Your savings account’s yield is a function of its interest rate and compounding frequency.

Compounding frequency describes how often your account adds the interest it’s earned to the original (principal) balance. The higher the compounding frequency, the longer each extra bit of interest has to earn interest on itself.

For example, imagine two seemingly identical savings accounts. Both earn 0.50% interest. The only difference: Account A compounds annually and Account B compounds daily.

You seed both accounts with $10,000 and make no further deposits. The interest rate remains level at 0.50%. By Year 10, how much bigger is Account B’s balance?

A whopping $1.31, that’s how much. After accounting for inflation, the difference is even smaller.

Federal deposit insurance (FDIC coverage) protects savings balances held with member FDIC institutions up to at least $250,000. That protection kicks in if the member bank fails.

Always ensure your bank is FDIC-insured. Otherwise, there’s no guarantee you’ll get your money back if it closes its doors.

FDIC insurance doesn’t cover everything that can go wrong at your bank. It might not reimburse you if your account is hacked and drained without your consent or if you fall victim to a financial scam.

Some banks continue to charge excess withdrawal fees. But a growing number of financial institutions now choose to waive them.

That’s because of a long-overdue change to a Federal Reserve bylaw known as Regulation D (Reg D). For years, Reg D limited withdrawals or payments from savings and money market accounts to six per statement period.

In April 2020, the Federal Reserve announced that deposit institutions were no longer bound by the strict monthly withdrawal limit.

FDIC-insured high-yield savings accounts are completely safe, insuring your funds for up to $250,000, with some banks offering even higher levels of protection.

The best high-yield savings accounts also take extensive measures to protect your private information

Choosing a high-yield savings account can feel overwhelming, so take a step back before you make your pick and consider which factors matter most to you.

Often, the decision process begins and ends with yield. If that’s the case for you, choose the highest-yielding savings account you can find.

Try not to overthink it. Opening a savings account isn’t something to be done lightly, but it’s also not as big a deal as buying a car or house. You can always open another one if you decide your first choice wasn’t the right one.

#8403. Dhaulagiri: Rope Fixing Halted For Unclear Reasons

About 20 climbers from several teams had planned to start their summit push on Dhaulagiri today, and conditions couldn’t be better: bluebird skies, low wind, and setting snow. So why are climbers stuck at Camp 2? And why are they so angry?

“We are…stuck here at Camp 2 waiting for the route above us to be fixed,” Paul Clarke of Australia texted to ExplorersWeb this morning.

As Clarke explained, the Sherpa team from Seven Summit Treks assigned to fix the route on Dhaulagiri this year refuses to lay ropes on the last sections above Camp 3.

“From what we are being told here at Camp 2, SST’s VVIP clients are no longer planning to climb higher,” Clarke said. “As a result, the company has little motivation to continue fixing the route for the remaining climbers.

The rope-fixing team had laid ropes until some 400m above Camp 3 earlier last week. The SST leader, Makalu Sherpa, shared his latest update on Friday. At that time, he reported everything was going well. The rope-fixing team made good progress while the clients waited at Camp 2. Neither SST nor 14 Peaks Expeditions has updated about Dhaulagiri since then. There have been no safety concerns reported during the current push.

In recent years, 8,000m peaks have been fixed either by a dedicated team assigned by the Expedition Operators Association of Nepal or by agreement among the companies on the mountain. They assign the rope fixing to a team of volunteers, whom the other operators all chip in to pay. Most 8,000m clients these days lack the skills to climb on their own and depend entirely on fixed ropes (and a packed trail) prepared by Sherpas.

The assigned rope-fixing team may stop for safety reasons, such as bad weather or risky conditions. We are waiting for further statements to clarify the situation. For now, unless a different group of Sherpas takes over, there will be no summit push.

This has frustrated those like Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha of Hungary. The pair patiently remained at Base Camp during the storm two weeks ago and have been at Camp 2 for five days, waiting for their moment. It’s mid-October, and there will probably be no further opportunities for them.

Today, Anni Penttila of Finland posted a text in Finnish on Instagram that translates to:

“Nothing came of it this time, either. It’s so disappointing that there’s really nothing to say at this point. Everyone turned back to Base Camp today.”

Anni Penttila’s story today from Dhaulagiri.

As the clients all retreat, Andrzej Bargiel remains at Base Camp with his large support and film team. The Polish skier intends to climb and ski down Dhaulagiri without oxygen. He has already skied eight other 8,000m peaks in that style, including Everest.

#8402. Beware, A Disability Can Force You Into Early Retirement

Earlier this year, I was sick for two weeks. Unfortunately, I’ve had asthma since I was a kid. So when a respiratory illness hits, I tend to cough and suffer longer than the average person.

During COVID, my asthma flared up more often, likely due to the stress of having a baby during a pandemic.

It’s the type of breathing where you’re annoyingly conscious of every breath. You can never quite fill your lungs to 100%. In my case, it felt more like 75%.

On Wednesday, August 12, still sick, I decided to keep a previously scheduled consulting call with an FS reader. I had booked it assuming I’d be better by then. I wasn’t.

By the end of our 1 hour, 15 minute session, where I spent about 80% of the time talking, I was wiped out. My energy had dropped to maybe 30%. When you’re talking nonstop, you’re not breathing deeply or regularly. I felt like I was slowly suffocating while discussing their asset allocation.

The call reminded me of the many days I felt physically drained talking to clients during my 13 years in finance. As my responsibilities and stress grew, I eventually hit a breaking point. I’d rather earn nothing and be free and healthy than keep grinding myself down.

Just the other day, I couldn’t bend down to pick something up without a sharp pain shooting through my spine. I almost collapsed.

The last time I felt pain this bad was in 2023. I had spent an hour sitting on the ground signing copies of Buy This Not That for readers who donated to victims of the Maui fires. My dad is from Hawaii, and seeing thousands of lives upended overnight weighed on me. The Financial Samurai community ended up donating about $48,000. But when the signing was over, I couldn’t stand up and I called my wife for help.

My theory is that these episodes are triggered by a combination of prolonged stress and me forgetting I’m not 25 anymore.

This time, I clearly forgot. On Sunday, I played two hours of 4.5-level pickleball, then taught my kids for another hour. On Monday, I played 1.5 hours of intense tennis with plenty of serving. Then on Tuesday, several dads in our dad bod challenge shared their gym Personal Records, so naturally I went for personal records too. Instead of my usual three sets of 10-12 reps, I did five sets with progressive loading.

Wednesday morning, my back was already grumbling. So of course I went on a hilly 30-minute walk at 7:05am before breakfast and the school drop off. Walking downhill to school, the pain returned. By the time I got home, I could no longer walk normally.

If I still had a day job, there’s no way I could have gone into the office. And if my asthma flared up at the same time, I couldn’t speak to clients for more than an hour or two a day.

Not being able to provide for my family would be a terrible thing.

These two episodes forced me to confront a few uncomfortable truths:

Some people picture disability as a dramatic car accident or a fall off a ladder. Reality is far more boring. Accidental injuries make up only about 9% to 12% of long-term disability claims, while musculoskeletal problems like back and joint pain are the leading cause, at 26% to 33% of claims.

According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), roughly one in four 20-year-olds will be out of work for at least a year because of a disabling condition before reaching normal retirement age. That’s one quarter of all 20-year-olds, not just those in high-risk occupations.

In other words, the thing that takes you out of the workforce probably won’t be a skydiving mishap. It’ll be your back after one too many weightlifting attempts.

Before getting into what to do, it’s worth understanding the two main types of disability coverage. They work very differently.

Short-term disability (STD) covers you for a temporary inability to work, like recovering from surgery, a bad back, or a serious illness. Benefits typically replace around 50% to 70% of your income and last anywhere from a few weeks to about six months. The waiting period, called the elimination period, is usually short, often one to two weeks.

Many employers provide short-term disability as a benefit. A handful of states also run their own programs, including California (SDI), New York, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Hawaii (TDI). If you’re self-employed, you probably have nothing unless you bought it yourself.

Long-term disability (LTD) kicks in when a disability lasts longer, usually after a 90-day elimination period. It typically replaces about 60% of your income and can pay for a set number of years or until age 65. This is the coverage that actually protects your family’s financial future. Short-term disability is a speed bump. Long-term disability is a car crash.

And no, don’t count on Social Security Disability Insurance to save you. SSDI is hard to qualify for, has a five-month waiting period, and the monthly benefit is modest. It’s a floor, not a plan.

If you have a job with benefits, log into your HR portal today and look at your LTD coverage. Many group policies cap monthly benefits, which means high earners may only be replacing a fraction of their income.

If there’s a gap, buy a supplemental individual policy, ideally with an own-occupation rider. It’s portable, so it stays with you if you leave your job. If you’re self-employed like me, individual LTD is the only coverage you’ll have. Get quotes while you’re young and healthy, because pre-existing conditions get excluded or priced up later.

Even with great coverage, there’s a gap. Short-term disability might make you wait a week or two, and long-term disability usually makes you wait 90 days. Meanwhile, your mortgage, tuition, and Costco runs don’t pause.

Keep at least six months of living expenses in cash or Treasury bills. If you have kids, a single income household, or are self-employed, aim for 12 months. If you’re wondering where the line is between prudent and paranoid, here’s my take on how much savings is too much. The emergency fund is your bridge from healthy to covered.

A single income stream is a single point of failure. If that engine stalls, the whole plane goes down. Your goal is to build a jet with at least four engines, so you can lose one and still land safely.

The best time to start a side hustle is while you still have a steady paycheck and good health. You get to experiment without pressure, and if it fails, you still eat.

I started Financial Samurai in July 2009 while working full-time in finance. I’d wake up early and write before work, then publish again on weekends. For three years, it made very little money. But by the time I left Corporate America in 2012, the site had become a real second engine alongside about $80,000 a year in passive investment income.

Without that second engine, I never would have had the courage to negotiate my way out.

Here’s the key for disability planning: prioritize side hustles that don’t require your body to show up. Driving for Uber or coaching tennis stops the moment your back gives out. Writing, a blog, a YouTube channel, an online course, or a self-published ebook can keep paying while you’re flat on your back.

If you need ideas, my wife put together a list of the 20 best side hustle ideas to make extra money. If you want to go the online route, here’s how to start a blog and build your own platform. I’m biased, but owning your own corner of the internet is the gift that keeps on giving.

One engine is a job. Two engines is a cushion. Four or more engines is freedom.

Your peak earning years are also, conveniently, your peak health years. Don’t assume your income will keep climbing forever. Assume it could drop to zero tomorrow, then save as if that’s true.

Related: Achieving FI With A Visual Impairment

I saved over 50% of my after-tax income starting with my first job out of college because I knew I couldn’t last a lifetime working 70+ hours a week. I didn’t know my lungs and back would eventually join the protest, but the logic held up.

Front-load your savings. Max out your 401(k) and IRA, and invest the excess in a taxable brokerage account. Pay down high fixed costs where you can.

The lower your required monthly expenses, the less income replacement you need if disaster strikes. A paid-off house is one of the best disability insurance policy nobody talks about.

Your ability to earn over the next 20 to 30 years is likely worth millions. Yet we manage our portfolios more carefully than our bodies.

Get annual checkups. But lock down a life insurance policy before you see a doctor for something more. Manage your stress before it manages you. Warm up, cool down, and stop trying to beat the other dads’ PRs after a weekend of nonstop racquet sports. Ask me how I know.

While you’re at it, get your paperwork in order. A will, a durable power of attorney, and a healthcare directive are the basics. But if anyone depends on your income, term life insurance is the most important piece. A disability takes away your ability to earn for a while. Death takes it away for good.

The irony is that the health problems that make you worry about disability also make life insurance more expensive, or harder to get. Lock in coverage while you’re still healthy enough to qualify. I’d compare term life quotes on Policygenius, which lets you see prices from multiple top insurers in one place.

The scary thing about disability is that it rarely announces itself. One day you’re serving aces and going for gym PRs. The next, you can’t walk your kids to school.

Being unable to breathe normally or walk for a few days made me realize how fragile everything is. If you’re the provider for your family, that fragility is your responsibility to plan for.

So check your disability coverage this week. Build your cash buffer. Start a side hustle that doesn’t depend on your body showing up. And for goodness sake, stretch.

Have you ever been unable to work for an extended period due to an illness or injury? Do you know whether your employer’s long-term disability policy is own-occupation or any-occupation, and when it switches? How many engines of income do you have today, and which would keep running if you couldn’t get out of bed? Have you bought supplemental disability insurance, or do you think it’s a waste of money? And what side hustle would you start if your main income disappeared tomorrow?

To get new posts in your inbox as soon as they’re published, ad-free for the first few hours, sign up for the free Financial Samurai newsletter here. Join 60,000+ readers building wealth and breaking free sooner.

This post is about how quickly your ability to earn can disappear. The best defense is building wealth and multiple income streams during your healthiest years, before your back and lungs start filing complaints.

That’s exactly what I lay out in my USA Today bestseller, Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures. I’ve distilled 30 years of experience studying, working in, and writing about personal finance into a roadmap for reaching $1 million and beyond, while you still have the energy to enjoy it.

Get a copy today. Your future self, possibly lying flat on the floor with a bad back, will thank you.

I had a concussion which another cyclist collided into me over a decade ago. I was 54 yrs. I lost my memory for 4 hrs. and have no memory of people helping to get off bike path, transported by ambulance to hospital, etc. It was like the movies…I woke up in pain and was on a spinal bord in ICU ward, with my partner and neurology dr. bending over, testing my memory after I awoke. I had to learn to walk slowly in lst few wks., I was dizzy just standing in the shower or in front of my kitchen sink, turning. I had to rest for many hours in bed for well over a month. If I walked too fast, I got dizzy from seeing blur of colours of scenery around me, etc. Thankfully as part of employer’s benefit, I had short-term disability insurance which I had to tap into long-term disability insurance. I returned to work lst part-time after 5 months on disability /medical leave. I returned to cycling slowly at 6 months. My partner did all the housework, cooking and food shopping during my recovery. It took me another few additional months to become comfortable even having other cyclists cycle around me.

It scared the beejesus out of me, because I solo paying off my home mortgage. My partner was still paying off his. This is what happens when you are solely responsible for your own mortgage or any huge loan/debt. Your financial vulnerability becomes even more acutely real. I so strongly recommend any worker get disability insurance..and if you don’t have children, you don’t have to worry about life insurance. There’s far greater likelihood during your working years, you will not prematurely die young but more likely to have major injury/ surgery (broken leg, hip replacement, etc.) that will sideline you from your job for a few months or a yr. All of us, even the most healthy (like myself) will experience a major injury/illness where we can’t do our money-earning job.

Sam, this article really hit home for me. At age 55, I began experiencing symptoms of an extremely rare disease. After years of uncertainty, dozens of doctors, and losing nearly 40 pounds, I suffered a stroke at 57 that abruptly ended my career in construction management and real estate development. Fortunately, the stroke spared my speech, cognition, and memory, but permanently impaired my left-side motor control and sensation. Thirteen years later, chronic pain, spasticity, and mobility limitations remain daily challenges. One lesson I’d emphasize is the importance of good health insurance. Medical bills totaled approximately $675,000 over four years, including $485,000 leading up to and including the stroke. Even with insurance, some rehabilitation required appeals or out-of-pocket payments. My stroke also forced me to sell my interest in our development business to my longtime partner. Although we had planned for a buyout in the event of death, disability was a different matter, and we ultimately negotiated an amicable agreement. I was fortunate to have accumulated substantial savings and investments before becoming disabled. Equally important, I was blessed with supportive family and friends, including a sister who’s a professional financial advisor, a physician brother-in-law, a daughter who’s an ER nurse, and a son who’s a mental health therapist. Unable to return to work, I focused more on managing our investments. With my sister’s guidance, we maintained a buy-and-hold approach through major market downturns. I’m a testament to time in the market, not timing the market, and the power of compounding. Our net worth has more than tripled since before the stroke. Meanwhile, rehabilitation remains a lifelong project. Now 71, I recently returned to my longtime neurological physical therapist after a three-year break. I’m still looking for ways to improve my independence, mobility, and quality of life. Forced retirement at 57 certainly didn’t mean the end of a productive and purposeful life. Financial independence can’t restore your health, but it provides options when life changes unexpectedly. My advice: Save and invest early, maintain good insurance, appreciate your support network, and don’t postpone enjoying life while you’re healthy.

Thank you for sharing your experience. It really hits Home, the importance of good health, good health insurance, and spending more intentionally with our one and only lives.

I wish you good health and prosperity. Don’t be a stranger!

#8401. Kyrgyz Climb 'Eternal Flame' Route on Nameless Tower

On September 28, a Kyrgyz team made its country’s first ascent of 6,239m Nameless Tower.

The expedition was led by Mikhail Mikhailov, known for his role in the 2004 North Face ascent of Jannu, which earned a Piolet d’Or, and for the 2009 first ascent of Peak 6134 on Minya Konka with Alexander Ruchkin, according to Mountain.ru.

Other members of the Nameless Tower group include Mikhail Danichkin, Timur Akbashev, Aidar Akbashev, Zarina Kutanova, and Aleksei Pototsky. The Kyrgyz team carried out the technical climb of this soaring granite spire, one of the Trango Towers, via the famous Eternal Flame route.

Nameless Tower. Photo: Timur Akbashev/Mountain.ru

Eternal Flame is one of the most celebrated big-wall routes in the Karakoram. It was first climbed in September 1989 by Kurt Albert, Wolfgang Gullich, Christof Stiegler, and Milan Sykora on Nameless Tower’s South Face. The original climbing route is roughly 650m long, on a vertical wall with a total height of about 1,000m. It was graded VI, 7b+, A2.

The route combines sustained hard granite climbing with the altitude, logistics, and objective hazards of a 6,000m Karakoram peak, which is why it has remained a major objective for both free climbers and traditional alpinists. The Kyrgyz ascent adds its country’s name to the short list of teams that have summited by this classic line.

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8399. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Adventure Has No Retirement Age: Adventure is continuing well into the ninth decade of life for a growing number of paddlers and hikers. Ninety-one-year-old Dale “Greybeard” Sanders only took up extreme endurance challenges at 80. Since then, he has paddled the Mississippi River from source to sea twice, completed the Missouri River Race, and this year reclaimed the record as the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail.

The challenge of competing and breaking records keeps him going, but not everyone is chasing endurance records. For Wendy Eden, 77, the goal is just to be out in nature and to keep exploring her beloved Canadian wilderness on her own. That means adapting her approach as she gets older.

I Hitchhiked From Sydney to Perth: Aston Brown describes his experience of hitchhiking across Australia from Sydney to Perth. He sees hitchhiking as an opportunity to surrender control and connect with people he would otherwise never meet.

Far more common in the 1970s and 1980s, the practice plummeted in Australia because of its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who targeted hitchhikers. Now it is starting to pick up again, as online communities and social media introduce it to a new generation.

Brown recognizes that hitchhiking carries dangers and that his experience as a man does not reflect the risks women traveling alone face. Yet his journey left him with a sense of connection. He spent three days and 1,900km traveling with Neil, a 79-year-old widower, on a four-month road trip around Australia. He also met a Zimbabwean family who had left the U.S. because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns, a retired tractor enthusiast, and Doug, head of Australia’s national science agency, who invited him birdwatching to see one of the country’s rarest birds.

She Had a Will To Live: A 72-year-old hiker survived six nights in the wilderness after falling 30m down a steep embankment. Mary Beth Granbery was on the Cabin Creek Trail near Mount Shasta in California when she fell.

She had set out on a multi-day camping trip and was expected home within four days. When she failed to return, friends and family raised the alarm. Rescuers found her camper van at the trailhead and launched a search. They found her one day later, at the bottom of the embankment. Despite suffering injuries from the fall, dehydration, and hypothermia from the cool nights, Granbery was still conscious when the rescue team reached her.

Across Madagascar To Find The World’s Last Lemurs: Geena Truman and her husband took a 2,500km road trip across Madagascar to search for lemurs. In a rented 4×4, they set off from Antananarivo. On the RN7 highway, they drove through rainforest, highland rice paddies, canyons, and desert, encountering rare species including golden bamboo lemurs, ring-tailed lemurs, and Verreaux’s sifakas.

Leaving the highway, they ended up on rough tracks with tricky river crossings, mud pits, and routes so difficult to navigate that they hired a local guide, known as a pisteur, to find their way.

Driving through Madagascar’s iconic baobab trees towards Tsingy de Bemaraha and Kirindy Reserve. Photo: Geena Truman

Grand Ole Roadtrip: In the summer of 1976, six young climbers piled into a blue Ford van and drove west to tackle Wyoming’s Teton Range. That first trip to the Tetons saw them face loose rock on the Enclosure Ice Couloir, a terrifying slide down the Skillet Couloir that nearly carried two of the group over a glacier’s edge, and two separate encounters with violent thunderstorms that left them clinging to exposed rock.

At the heart of all of this was the Grand Teton Climbers’ Ranch (GTRC), an affordable base for mountaineers. It offered more than a cheap bed: It was a place to meet climbing partners, exchange stories, and recover from the day over shared meals. Today, the GTRC remains one of their favorite places on Earth.

Renate Powell Completes Munro Round in Barefoot Shoes: Renate Powell has completed her second round of Scotland’s 282 Munros, this time in barefoot shoes. The keen hillwalker turned to minimalist footwear in her forties when an old skiing injury left her knee in constant pain.

She started by walking just 100m a day, then spent more than a year gradually building up to take on a Munro in her barefoot shoes. Fourteen years after first trying them, she continues her long-distance walking, without the knee replacement that was initially suggested.

Climbing the Cuillin Munro in barefoot shoes. Photo: Gillian Parker

Mad, Bad and Dangerous To Know: Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, has been living with Parkinson’s for seven years. He’s been out of the public eye for two years, and his current state is uncertain.

Fiennes spent much of his life building a remarkable expedition career after serving in the military. His 1979-82 Transglobe Expedition saw him and fellow former SAS soldiers Charles Burton and Oliver Shepard complete a 60,000km circumnavigation using surface travel, crossing both Poles.

He later completed a 2,170km unsupported ski crossing of Antarctica with Mike Stroud, and attempted to reach the North Pole unsupported five times. After severe frostbite during a 2000 expedition, he famously amputated his own dead fingertips with a fretsaw. This article plots out the timeline of his extraordinary expeditions.

A Climber Has Now Called For Help Three Times in 2026: Two climbers had to be rescued on September 22 after becoming stranded on the 500m White Dyke scramble on British Columbia’s Edge Peak. The pair set out at 8:30 am, but later that afternoon, with only three hours until sunset, the less experienced climber was too exhausted to continue.

After two hours attempting to rescue themselves, they activated a Garmin SOS beacon. This is the third time one of the climbers in the duo has had to be rescued this year. Rescue veteran Brent Boulet warned that social media seems to be drawing less experienced people onto technical routes. He stressed the importance of realistic timing, turning back when necessary, and knowing a climbing partner’s capabilities before setting out.
