#8316. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

For nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it showed Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

In the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first important Italian treatise on the subject.

Vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:

“The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library

Sella’s most important Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

Muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

The peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella

Sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

From other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

Muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

The French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

On July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly showed the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

They fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

After the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

The two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

Far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

The southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal

Since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

In August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal

Four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a new route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

The 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal

#8311. Weekend Warm-Up: First Descent Rio Cuervo

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

With an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson launches into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

Forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

The team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot

The dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to plan ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

When they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

Sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

The contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

Early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”

This movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8307. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Lara Neumeier Makes First Female Ascent of a 5.14c: On October 7, Lara Neumeier made the first female ascent of Rhapsody (E11 7a/5.14c) at Dumbarton Rock, Scotland. She succeeded 20 years after Dave MacLeod established the route as the world’s first E11.

Neumeier’s ascent makes her the fifth woman to climb a 5.14c trad route. In an interview, she discussed the 15 climbing days and two visits spent working the route, how it compares to other routes, and her hope that the ascent will encourage more women to attempt the iconic line.

Karl Bushby, shortly after starting and now. Photo Facebook

I Left My 8-Year-Old Son Behind 28 Years Ago to Walk Around the World: After 28 years walking around the world, Karl Bushby should complete this Goliath Expedition within the next month. Now he faces an emotional homecoming: his son, whom he left behind at the age of eight, is now 36. Bushby has a grandchild he has never met, and his mother has seen him only three times since he left.

Julia Clarke hikes beside a stream in Mull, Scotland. Photo: Julia Clarke

Here are Nine British Hiking Rules Americans Need to Know: After returning to Scotland after more than a decade in Colorado, Julia Clarke realized she needed to rethink her mountain skills. She warns Americans not to underestimate the weather, terrain, or seemingly puny hills in Britain.

From wild camping rules and differences in hiking trails, to avoiding cows and brushing up on your navigational skills, she shares nine key differences American hikers should understand before tackling the British backcountry.

Women Across Diving Speak Out on Harassment: Women across the diving industry are speaking out about sexual harassment and assault. After years of raising concerns, petitioning and reporting to expedition operators and dive agencies with little outcome, many are taking to social media to share the experiences that have affected their careers as instructors, expedition leaders, and marine professionals.

Campaigners are demanding that the industry establish better and more accessible reporting systems, better safeguarding standards, and that operators vet their staff properly.

The Art of Progress: Climbing ethics are constantly evolving, and many are now reconsidering whether traditional ground-up ascents, minimal bolting, and preserving the original character of a route should take precedence over safety, accessibility, and the experience of future climbers.

Derek Franz explores this debate by looking at lines across Yosemite, Madagascar, Germany, and Patagonia, and the work underway to replace corroded bolts in many of them. The approach challenges the idea that a first ascent should remain untouched.

Three Dead After Avalanche in Chile: On October 17, an avalanche swept seven mountaineers into Laguna del Inca near Chile’s Ski Portillo resort. Three were killed and four injured.

The group was climbing toward Cerro Los Tres Hermanos when they triggered a slab avalanche. Rescue teams and the police responded within 10 minutes, and the survivors were airlifted to hospital. According to resort management, the group had entered a restricted area marked as an avalanche danger zone despite earlier warnings.

Old Traditions and New Developments on Mt. Kenya: Giovanni Trambaiolo explores Mount Kenya’s climbing history, especially the overlooked contributions of Kenyan climbers and the mountain’s deep spiritual significance to indigenous communities. He describes opening up Rainmaker, the new six-pitch trad route on the Temple Cliffs of Mount Kenya.

Three Mountain Emergencies in 14 Hours: Three hunting emergencies in northwest Colorado prompted search-and-rescue crews to respond within 14 hours, as the first significant snowfall of the season coincided with the opening of elk season on October 14 and 15.

Their first rescue call was for an overdue hunter, and the second from an individual who became separated from their group near Bears Ears and was too cold to walk. A third hunter suffered serious injuries when a tree fell on their tent as they slept. Another hunting party did not require rescue but got caught in snow, mud, and fog and spent over four hours finding their way back to camp.

#8303. Couple Cycle America's New Golden Gravel Trail

Colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

The Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association

Stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”

The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Big Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Big Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com

Likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly important in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”

#8301. Zero In Fishkill, NY

In the return to my usual schedule of taking Sundays off the reality of reaching the closing stages of my hike start to sink in.

Phew! It has been 8 days since my last zero. It was a bold call to change up my normal routine and take a Friday off but it couldn’t have worked out better. I avoided a wet day on trail, then had 8 straight dry days to make up for the lost hiking time. With this weekend’s F1 Grand Prix taking place in Austin, Texas I had a distraction free morning to work on the blog thanks to the 4:00PM EST race start time. I saw my first and so far only Grand Prix in person at the race track in Austin, known as the Circuit of the Americas. I added a few photos from that visit to this blog to spice it up a bit.

This post will publish November 2nd! I am nearly in the final month of my hike, we are getting down to the wire now. I created an itinerary for the upcoming week and took a rough cut at setting my itinerary for the remaining weeks. It definitely looks I am on track to complete the hike before Thanksgiving, ideally the weekend before. I still would like a little more buffer to allow for at least one break-glass-in-case-of-emergency off day should I need it over the next few weeks.

I am finally starting to appreciate my own work on the blog. I haven’t ever done something like this before. Scrolling through my pages of blog posts, I feel that I have put together something remarkable. At the same time I can’t help but feel that I am a sort of proxy to all this. I didn’t create the amazing terrain, I just tapped a button on my phone to capture a photo of it. I didn’t create The Trek or WordPress in order to make everything look polished, I just sat at my laptop uploading the content. I feel lucky that we live in a time where documenting and sharing a journey like mine is easier than ever.

The COTA Observation Tower at the US Grand Prix when I visited in 2022.

A Red Bull F1 car circulates the track at the US Grand Prix when I visited in 2022.

I wasn’t feeling at my best heading into the 8 day stretch but, thanks to relatively flat trail conditions, I was able to get the miles done that I needed and then some. Across the 8 days, I hiked 198.6 miles. I even found time to stay slightly more on top of taking notes for my blog to keep less work for myself on my off day. I can’t ask for a better week than that!

It should be a manageable week coming up. The terrain looks relatively flat, similar to this past week. The biggest issue may be the cold, most nights will be in the 30s, some approaching freezing temperatures. For now I plan to hike 3 2-day backpacking stints, so I would spend 3 nights on the trail in my tent. Expect more posts critiquing the existence of seasons in the coming week 😉

#8298. Climber Falls to Death on Ama Dablam

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence shows he fell 1,700m to his death.

Waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

Climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa

According to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 showed that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

Virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

The upper part of Ama Dablam at sunset. Photo: 8K Expeditions

#8294. New Cyclone Approaches Nepal

For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

#8287. Mont Blanc Has Grown Almost Two Meters — But Not in the Way You Think

These days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps. But strangely, Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, has grown significantly since its latest measurement in 2023.

Mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute). The new official altitude is now 4,807.47 meters (15,772.5 feet) above sea level.

However, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides. Measurements are carried out every two years, and each time the registered altitude varies:

Graphic showing the results of the last few measurements on Mont Blanc, by LaChangingMeteo

Mont Blanc’s “summit is constantly shifting,” Jean des Garets, chief geometer in the Haute-Savoie department, told Le Monde.  “Each individual measurement is not significant in itself.”

So, what’s with the yearly differences? Obviously, it’s the variation in the thick but ever-changing snowcap that covers the summit.

The mountain’s rocky summit measures around 4,792m above sea level. The snow cover varies with the seasons. The difference from the previous measurement shows that 2023 was much drier at summit altitude.

The survey team on itsir way to the summit of Mont Blanc.. Photo: ING

A team from the Order of Chartered Surveyors (Ordre des géomètres-experts) acclimatized first by climbing Bishorn (4,153m). They then spent some days measuring several points around the mountain. Finally, they climbed Mont Blanc via the normal route on September 15-16.

Once on top, they pinpointed the highest point using a GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) pole, which measures altitude in real time.

The recent survey featured an interesting novelty. In addition to altitude, the survey also measured Mont Blanc’s gravity by installing a gravimeter on the summit for the first time ever. This measured the force with which the Earth attracts the device. In so doing, they wanted to determine whether the summit has sunk, regardless of ice cover.

The gravimeter on the summit of Mont Blanc, September 16. Photo: ING France

“When the height of Mont Blanc changes, we can’t know for sure whether the ground or the rock has moved or if the ice has melted,” explains Olivier Jamet.

Gravity provides the missing information: mass. If the ice has melted, there is less material under the instrument, but the rock has moved closer to it. Distinguishing these two effects requires a model of the ice cap and the massif, and above all, repeated measurements at the same location. And the effort is worthwhile, especially now that the effects of climate change on Alpine glaciers are becoming increasingly apparent.

The gravimeter on the top of Mont Blanc measured the gravity at 9.7944689 m/s².

“For comparison, this value is 9.81 m/s² in Marseille (located at sea level) and 9.8043046 m/s² in Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet (580m above sea level),” ING reports. “This difference in value, even if it seems small, allows for the detection of changes in mass, particularly in the mass of the ice. Repeated over time, these gravity measurements will thus contribute to improving the determination of the altitude of the highest peak in Western Europe.”

#8286. The Continental Divide Trail: The Southern Terminus

Cold, orange sky. Shapeless clouds. Nothing to imagine. Ice Cream looked out into that sky, imagining anyway, letting her mind swirl with past and present and future.

She turned her neck back briefly toward Zen, still sleeping on the sand, cutely wrapped in his quilt, and then looked again at the pastel sky and waited for the first slice of burning sun to rise above the desert. She always woke first. Sometimes she would lay there reading while Zen breathed deeply with dreams. But today was not for reading. Today was the final day of the CDT. Nearly six months, over two thousand miles, and enough experiences to stretch that time out into years of memory. She let those memories flash, pulling gently at their threads, weaving them into a tapestry in her mind. Years from now, sitting around a fire at Trail Days, her friends would ask her how she remembered so much and she would tell them that she didn’t know.

Zen opened his eyes, stretching and groaning happily. She smiled at him and lay her hand on his cheek. “My sweet.”

He sat up. “I won’t sit around too long. I know you want to walk in this.”

The sun followed its arc. Apollo roared in his fiery and predictable chariot toward high noon. The morning colors turned baby blue. And the shadows became harsh. And the warm wind blew. Underfoot the desert was pushed back step by step until the corrugated steel of a shade structure came into view, and next to that, a small monument. The stone stood stone still, a Washington Monument in miniature, a symbol of all that’s good in the American spirit–that fire that brought people hurtling across the seas toward either a better life or else death. And here now was a daughter of that spirit, having braved what she could in a world where nothing was left unexplored. Nothing but her mind, her heart. But inner worlds can still be traveled to by foot, and she had traveled them.

“There it is!” Ice Cream said. Her pace picked up and Zen followed. She approached the monument. Perhaps not with reverence, but certainly with something. She touched it carefully at first, just one tentative finger, Sistine Chapel like. The stone still held the cold of night.

Toolman was already there and he got up from his spot in the shade. “Y’all want your picture?”

“Yes!” Ice Cream and Zen posed as hikers always do, and then they did another thing that hikers always do — they sat on their asses in the shade.

Institute was already there, too. “Congratulations.”

“You too!” Ice Cream said. “We did it.” She got up and went to the loose barbed wire fence that was the border between the US and Mexico and she looked out. It was just a farm there. Just a normal life in another world. “I could just walk over there,” she mused to herself. “Probably wouldn’t make it very far, but… I don’t know. I could.” She stepped back over the fence onto her own soil, went back to the shade and waited.

Not too long later Frito arrived and group photos were taken and then more sitting and waiting. Frito laid out his rocks, lovingly. He’d collected at least another ten pounds. Toolman kicked back on his pack, one knee over the other. Zen lit up his last bowl of weed in the pipe he’d found on a mountaintop in Montana, and then, when the bowl was empty, he took it and placed it on the top of a post, nestled where it wouldn’t fall. “There,” he said. “I hope someone finds it and takes it back to Montana.”

The shuttle came. When it did, Ice Cream chose the bed of the truck this time. Zen rode with her. He always chose the bed if he could. The desert rolled away in dust. The road was rocky for miles and then suddenly, a smooth, black highway. The shuttler pulled into an eclectic gas station. Ice Cream and Crew went in one last time to buy ice cream and cold drinks and whatever snacks they could find, chatting up the station owner and a few locals. “I saw a sasquatch,” one of them said. “It was hairless, like one of those hairless cats and it ran on all fours. Its arms were long.”

Ice Cream took a bite of her ice cream and nodded along. She wanted to believe him and so she did believe. Belief was sometimes as simple as that. And she looked toward Zen and rolled her eyes at his rakish grin and probing questions. “How many miles an hour would you say it was running? Did it ever stand up on two legs? How tall would you say it was?”

She left Zen to his sasquatchian interrogations and wandered around the station, seeing all the strange and magical items mixed in with the mundane. A genie lamp next to a hunter’s fleece. A wizard staff hanging on the wall next to the quarts of motor oil.

“One of my neighbors died,” the station owner said as she observed. “We ended up with all this stuff. Couldn’t believe some of it. But who knows where it’s going next. We’re selling this place. Not sure if they’ll keep it.”

“Shame,” Ice Cream said, not having words for why, but feeling it powerfully nonetheless. And that was her soul. A knowing soul, but no part of her could bring its mind to her tongue. She went to the corkboard and read the local messages. Puppies for sale. Tractors for sale. Handymen and babysitters looking for work. And there, pinned in the top left corner, an envelope. Not knowing why, she took it. Inside was a folded paper, letter-like. Her hands quivered ever so slightly as she unfolded the yellowed page and written there at the top it said:

The mountains miss your face. Shadows fall on cold rock And dim light drips from a dreary sun. But when you’re there The sun finds its purpose, the shadows become a wedding dress.

A wild meseta. It says to itself “I’ve seen this one before,” and lets you pass in quiet thought.

The mountains again. New and sharp. The sun grows weaker, the shadows colder, cozier. Climbing, scrambling, passing through thunder clouds, Breathing air that’s atom thin, you’re strong now As only mountains can make you.

The desert has forgotten you. But your spirit persisted there, dormant in saguaro flowers and bloomed in grey November.

And there at the border the desert goes ever on, to places with strange tongues and long-buried graves of dead priests. From those lands come tales of jungles and giant trees, even lands of fire. But these are not for you. Not yet.

Dear Fellow Travelers, This concludes The Continental Divide Trail. Thank you for joining Ice Cream and I on this adventure. We look forward to seeing you in the next one. Until then. Happy Trails and Buen Camino.

#8283. Walking and Canoeing from Kansas to the Gulf of Mexico

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

Robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

During the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

“The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

Cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They launched the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

It’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

#8279. Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 27

Most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents from the last seven days.

A tiger killed two farmers in separate incidents about five kilometers apart within 24 hours in the eastern corner of India’s Maharashtra state.

Sixty-year-old farmer Nana Kambadi was killed by a tiger while working in his field on Saturday evening. The following evening, Premila Mahadole, 40, was attacked while harvesting rice. Her body was later found in the field. Officials suspect it was the same tiger, but this has not been confirmed.

The back-to-back killings have thrown residents across the district into a panic, according to the Times of India. At this time of year, many are out in their fields harvesting rice at the edges of forests.

The death toll from human-animal conflicts in just this part of Maharashtra state has now risen to 35 in 2026, according to officials.

A family herd of wild Indian elephants. Photo: Shutterstock

An elephant killed a man who was trying to drive a herd of 23 elephants away from his village in Jharkhand state in eastern India. According to forest officials, the elephant seized Nicholas Topno, 40, with its trunk, dragged him nearly 500m, and trampled him. The herd, which included five calves, had been damaging crops in the area. Officials had been monitoring the movements for several days and warned residents not to approach. Our team has been monitoring its movement round the clock for the last five days, but some villagers still ventured close to the elephants,” forest officer Shekhar Singh told the Times of India. She suffered facial injuries and a broken right leg but remained conscious and was able to speak when taken to hospital. She survived. Because bear attacks continue to be a problem in many parts of Japan, officials have warned residents to avoid unnecessary outings. Members of a hunting association patrol the area, and students are either bused to school or driven by their parents. In the first incident, a herder named Abubakar Aden Dube Bute was grazing his calves when he happened upon a herd of elephants. He tried to flee but failed and sustained multiple serious injuries to his head, ribs, and legs. Later, 72-year-old Abdikher Sheikh Ibrahim, originally from Somalia, died on his way home from fetching water. Another man with him escaped unharmed. A Cape buffalo in Uganda. Fellow swimmer Mike Loewe told state broadcaster SABC that members of the open-water swimming group she belonged to brought the gravely injured woman ashore. A medic in the group tried to help, but she died at the scene. Officials have closed the beach.

#8277. 9 Backpacking Myths Debunked: Hitchhiking, Rain Gear, Norovirus, and Ursacks (BPR #381)

In today’s episode of Backpacker Radio presented by The Trek, brought to you by LMNT, we are joined by a couple of familiar faces- Katie and Elise- for a panel on backpacking myths that just refuse to die.

In this one, we cover the worst ways to blow your money for a thru-hike, why finding the perfect rain jacket might be a lifelong exercise in disappointment, discuss why carrying a satellite communicator doesn’t mean you can outsource your survival to the SOS button, we cover the assumption that thru-hikers are all trust fund babies, make the case that a weeklong backpacking trip can actually be harder than a multi-month thru-hike, and of course we delve into bean soup theory.

We wrap the show with Trek Propaganda on swapping a $600 ultralight tent for a 5.5-ounce tarp, a Question of the Day about how many syllables are too many for a trail name, a Triple Crown of unconventional pets we wish we could have, a new Sun Hoodie Review of a dirt cheap option that earns a high score despite fitting like a muumuu, and a Mailbag from our dear Rachel about the absurd amount of work that goes into keeping her feet blister-free.

#8275. “I Was Sure I Was Going to Be Mauled.” The Season the Grizzlies Went Crazy

Published Oct 23, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

It was a bad season for grizzlies. Maybe the warm, wet summer had something to do with it, but for whatever reason, the bears were uncharacteristically aggressive. I’d been coming to these Alaskan mountains for five to eight weeks each season for nearly a decade to hunt, fish and live in the wilderness. I had seen hundreds of grizzlies, but with few exceptions, they always had been timid or curious, seldom dangerous. I usually carried a bear tag, partly because if I was forced to kill one, I wanted to keep the hide (in my home state of Alaska, a bear killed in self-defense becomes the property of the state if you haven’t got a bear tag or if it isn’t taken in season). I also wanted a seven-foot bear. Grizzlies in the northern interior and Arctic survive largely on vegetation and don’t get as big as the salmon-fed coastal bears. A seven-footer was as good as you could expect to see.

The first part of my annual expeditions was reserved for sheep hunting with Cheri Flory, a friend who has taken several trophy-quality caribou and moose. After the tiny Cessna 185 had clattered to a white-knuckled stop on an almost too short, rocky river bar, we floated downriver for two days. From there we backpacked several more days up an unnamed river, swollen and angry from recent rains, into ram country.

When we arrived at my campsite, on a bench above the river, a large, dark grizzly was grazing placidly on blueberries exactly where I have pitched my tent for the last several years. We shouted and I fired the 7mm-08 into the air. As the shot echoed between sheer, limestone walls, the bear ran straight up a steep, scree slope and over a ridge 2,000 feet above. No surprise. That’s how they usually behaved.

In the next few days, we spotted several more bears near camp, and even though they all behaved as expected—they moved away once they sensed us—I was vaguely uneasy. That unease was almost a foreboding, and it lasted until the end of the expedition.

Early one morning, Cheri and I started from camp to find a band of rams I’d seen from a distance the day before. A quarter-mile downwind of the tent, she spotted a bear laying on his belly on a talus slope just above her. The bear lay with his chin on folded paws, apparently just waiting for us to go by (grizzlies have better eyesight than most people give them credit for, and this one could clearly identify us 300 yards away). I wasn’t particularly worried, and there was no reason to think this bear would be any different from the rest we’d seen. I hollered, cursing the bear and his relatives. It had no effect. I shouted again, and this time fired a shot over his head. He sat up and cocked his head at us, but didn’t show the slightest inclination to run. We shouted ourselves hoarse, and I fired several more shots, but it didn’t faze the bear. In fact, he seemed almost amused by it.

Possibly he’d had the same treatment in earlier years, and because he hadn’t suffered, was no longer afraid. Probably, too, the smell of our camp was just too intriguing to ignore. No matter how careful you might be, in a bear’s incredibly keen nose, there will always be the smell of food around even the cleanest camps.

We had to protect our gear and food, so we turned back to camp. A ruined camp would have been a serious matter—we had 300 miles of wilderness backpacking and river travel to civilization, and the journey would take us six weeks. The loss of camp would be just as serious, perhaps, as a mauling. After all, we had antibiotics, pain pills and stitching gear in case of a mauling, but no spare tent or sleeping bags.

The moment we turned for camp, the bear padded after us. I was startled by the maneuver. For some reason it was the last thing I expected, so I opened the bolt to be sure that I had a full magazine and one up the throat. As I jammed the bolt shut, I reflected grimly that though the 7mm-08 was a good sheep gun, it was hardly the stuff for a charging grizzly.

As the distance closed, the bear slowed, then stopped and began browsing on soapberry bushes. I was pretty sure that it was a ruse. He didn’t want a confrontation just yet and was testing us to see just what he had to deal with. We walked slowly toward camp, taking pains not to hurry, which might cause the bear to chase us. I watched over my shoulder and prodded Cheri along (she was more fascinated than worried by the bear’s antics, and at the most irritating times she insisted on pausing and watching). The bear stripped the soapberry branches, leaves and all, as if that was all he was interested in, but watched us out of the corner of his eye and edged closer as he fed. He was still testing us, still trying to find out just how far he could go.

A moment after we walked into camp, the grizzly trotted over the crest of the bench, following our trail like a bloodhound with his nose to the ground. He stopped, looked at us and the tent, then swaggered slowly forward in an exaggerated, side-to-side gait. I hoped it was all bluff, but grabbed an aluminum pot and pan and while banging away, went to meet the bear. If there was going to be trouble, I didn’t want it in camp, where Cheri could get hurt or the tent destroyed. He stopped. I could see the surprise in his expression, and he let me come. At 30 yards the sweat began to trickle down my forehead, despite a cool breeze, and my skin suddenly felt too tight. I thumbed off the safety as my heart pounded in my ears, and advanced again. Finally, to my immense relief, the bear gave, hesitantly at first, then turned and walked slowly off the bench, glaring back over his shoulder almost as if to say, “I’m not quite through. Yet.”

We watched the bear browse on soapberry bushes for hours. Several times I fired the 7mm-08 at rocks only feet from his nose in hopes of driving him off, but all he did was stare stupidly at the rock powder hanging in the air. He didn’t even flinch. He obviously wasn’t impressed, and he slowly began moving toward camp again.

Eventually, he edged to within 40 yards of the tent, and twice made short, bluff charges, probably hoping we’d abandon camp and leave him to his explorations. He made clear our choice, though: Either move camp or he’d force a showdown. I didn’t want to shoot him—bear season wouldn’t open for several weeks and there’d be a great deal of red tape with the fish and game department if I did. Besides that, I’d strangely developed an affection for the wayward bear. After all, we were the intruders, and it was his country.

We had tried every diplomatic means to diffuse a confrontation, and nothing worked, so we began breaking camp. Cheri was stuffing the tent into my backpack when, without warning, he charged. The bear came at a gallop, growling fiercely but still not as intensely as a full charge might be. But I knew if he pressed home there’d be no telling what might happen. I couldn’t take the chance, so I aimed low near his feet, hoping to change his mind. If that didn’t work, I’d have time enough for one more quick shot.

He rolled over at the muzzle blast, bawling and swatting at the air as I worked the bolt. He regained his feet and then stumbled off the bench toward the creek. He sat down 100 yards away and licked his paw and glared at us on the slope just above.

We quickly stuffed our few final items into the packs and started up-canyon. I brought up the rear and kept a close watch behind. We hadn’t gone a quarter of a mile when the bear was nosing around our just vacated campsite. He didn’t limp in the least—apparently, I’d stung his paw with ricocheted debris.

Two hours later, I glanced down the canyon, and the bear was following our trail a half-mile below, again with nose to the ground exactly like a bloodhound. I’m used to being the hunter, so it was more than a little unsettling to suddenly find myself being hunted by something so much larger and more powerful. Only if the 7mm-08 was used properly (it was seeming smaller and smaller all the time), could it equalize things. For a moment, I felt a bit like David, and the bear was Goliath—finesse vs. brute strength. Eventually, he closed the distance to about 200 yards and kept it there. Then, finally, as we crossed a high shale ridge and dropped into the next drainage, he quit following. I breathed a huge sigh of relief when I was relatively sure that he’d quit dogging us, but it was several nights before I slept soundly again, and even then I kept one ear open and a loaded rifle beside me.

The sheep hunt was successful. We saw a half-dozen more grizzlies and all behaved themselves, and two weeks later we trekked back down to the river where we had left our cache stored in steel drums. We had 250 miles of wilderness river to float as we hunted for moose and caribou on our way to our bush-village destination. In time, we collected a good moose and a huge caribou, spotted several more passive grizzlies, and on the lower part of the river toward the end of the expedition, came into flat country where spawned-out salmon littered beaches and gravel bars. Bear tracks were everywhere, and in two days we spotted six grizzlies as we floated. Each night I unloaded and heaved the 14-foot raft up onto the bank next to the tent and tied aluminum pans to a line so I’d hear if a bear came into camp (if anything happened to the inflatable raft, we’d be in dire trouble).

One evening, we pulled up at a likely looking campsite. I climbed the bluff to check it out, without a gun, as I usually do, and forced my way through a screen of willows into the shadowy spruce timber to look for a place to pitch the tent. I walked around for a moment, then heard a commotion behind me.

I was sure that it was just a surprised moose crashing off, but when I turned I was face to face with a large grizzly charging down on me through the dusk and thick trees. Spruce branches were flying like straw, and the ivory of his teeth were almost glowing in the gloom. Any bear chasing you is apt to seem huge, but this one was honestly a big bear.

I was unarmed and as helpless as I’ve ever felt. My chest tightened as I waited for the impact and the teeth tearing into me. I was as sure as I’ve ever been of anything that I was going to be mauled, as sure as a falling rock climber is sure he’ll hit the rocks below. I was so positive of a mauling that I’d accepted it and was already thinking beyond to Cheri waiting in the raft. She was an experienced wilderness hand (this was her third trip), and I felt sure that she could get out the four days or so left downriver to the native village. But what of the grizzly? Would Cheri get away?

“Cheri, get the gun!” I said in a loud voice that wasn’t quite shouting and that sounded like someone else, hoping she’d be able to protect herself when the bear was through with me. Immediately she shouted something back and the bear veered at 15 feet, almost disappearing momentarily behind a deadfall, thoroughly confused by the second voice from a different place. It gave me a chance, and I rushed through the willows and leaped off the bluff onto the raft, at the same time hissing, “Row!” This time I kept my voice low, feeling that if I said it any louder it would bring the grizzly down on us. Cheri leaned urgently into the oars, and a moment later we were out into the current. I was elated, flying on an adrenaline high and almost giddy with the sudden release of tension and unexpected reprieve. I was still alive, still in one piece, and incredibly surprised about it. A moment later, the bear was on the bank looking for us, and I was trying to free the rifle from the duffel. Bear season had opened by then, and I could have cheerfully shot this one because he’d frightened me badly enough to sprinkle my beard with a handful of my first gray hairs (at least I blame it on that, because they showed up several weeks later). But before I could free the gun, he was gone.

We floated downriver until well after dark, trying to get as far away from the bear as possible before pitching the tent. Neither of us slept much that night, and I awoke frequently, quickly breathing and sweating from visions of bristling, bloody-jawed grizzlies standing over me.

Late the next afternoon, we tied off the raft in an eddy and climbed a low hill to pick some blueberries for dessert that night. This time I took the rifle and kept a careful watch as Cheri picked. We talked, and I felt sure any bear in the area would hear us and would have plenty of time to move off. We worked slowly over the hill, and suddenly, just below, was another bear.

“Oh God, not again!” I thought, feeling the blood thicken behind my eyes. This bear was very blond, and he saw me at the same time I saw him. He stood abruptly on his hind legs—seeming to tower over us like those Hollywood bears in old “B” westerns—nose raised into the wind and head rocking quickly from side to side as he tried urgently to scent us. I worked the bolt and brought the rifle up. Cheri heard the hard, metal sound of the bolt and froze, knowing what it was without seeing it. There was that same brassy taste in my mouth, and I knew before the bear started that he’d charge. We were just too close; given the adult male grizzly’s disposition and ego, he had no choice. He dropped quickly to all fours with an explosive snorting-grunt and charged, the glossy blond fur on his shoulders and neck filling the riflescope as he rushed silently, intently, bounding across the spongy tundra and closing the distance faster than I would have believed. At the shot, he seemed to hang there and stare a moment, almost in surprise, before sagging into the blood-colored dwarf birch. Then it was silent, nothing moved or made a sound; I had the feel of a mouthful of flannel as I tried to wet my lips.

Only after I lowered the rifle and breathed again did Cheri stand up from where she’d been picking berries on hands and knees. Later, I realized it had taken a great deal of self-possession to freeze that way with a grizzly charging you and with your survival in someone else’s hands. The big grizzly lay motionless less than 20 feet away; the bullet had shattered the vertebrae just behind the skull. He squared just seven feet, a very large bear for the country, and his hide was spectacular. But I killed him because I had to, even though I now very much appreciate the trophy.

He smelled wine-sweet, the odor of the fermented blueberries around us, as I stood next to him letting the tension uncoil. Cheri and I were both strangely subdued that afternoon, standing on the blazing crimson, gold and green tundra.

Why the grizzlies had been short-tempered that season is anyone’s guess. I’m fairly certain that I could wander up there for the rest of my life without another serious bear encounter, let alone three charges within a few weeks. But despite that, I’ll now carry a gun whenever I’m in grizzly country, something I never did before unless I was actually hunting. And without trying too hard, I can see again the big, dark grizzly charging down on me in the dusky gloom of the forest as I stand unarmed and as helpless as I’ve ever been. As I relive it, my palms become clammy and my scalp prickles as I wait for the impact and the teeth.

That season, I learned that I wasn’t the most important, the most powerful, maybe not even the most deadly creature in that wilderness. I also learned humility.

I didn’t shake that foreboding, gloomy feel of doom until days after the chartered plane landed at my cabin on the Yukon River, when I was sleeping in sheets again, behind a heavy log wall.

#8274. U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

On the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”

“Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.
