#8272. The Sneaky Reason Hunters Sometimes Miss Easy Shots on Big Game

Published Oct 23, 2026 12:51 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

“I couldn’t have missed; the crosshairs were right on.” How often have you heard this pitiful phrase, or, lamenting a missed deer, uttered it yourself?

It may come as a shock, but the reason why some shots mysteriously miss their targets can be explained by the fact that the shooter does indeed clearly recall seeing the crosshairs when he pulled the trigger. The memory of having seen the crosshair, or reticle, may very well have resulted from the shooter having had to look for the reticle in the scope’s field of view and then deliberately overlay it on the target. That means that the shooter’s primary attention had been focused on the reticle rather than the target.

Any time your concentration is not on the target, a miss is in the making.

Does this mean that the reticle in some scopes — perhaps the one you use — can be wrong for the kind of hunting and shooting that it is used for? Exactly. Of all the factors that have to work together when you aim your scope-sighted rifle, shotgun or handgun, one of the most important — the reticle in your scope — is one of the least understood. Also, for reasons that I can only guess at, discussions and even supposedly learned writings about telescopic sights seldom do more than pay lip service to reticles.

Before I sat down to write this column, I thumbed through the half-dozen good books on shooting that have been written during the past half-century and found that although the authors describe different reticles, usually with tidy illustrations, no really helpful suggestions or worthwhile conclusions are offered.

The standard advice being, “Here they are boys; use the one that tickles your fancy.”

I was even more distressed when, upon rereading the chapters on telescopic sights in a couple of books that I’d written, I discovered that although I had outdone myself in describing the mechanics and technical aspects of scopes and reticles, I had largely failed to take the subject off the pages and put it in a real shooting situation. I hadn’t explained why one type of reticle can offer a solid advantage over another.

Scope makers themselves have likewise been of little help, mainly catering to popular trends in reticles and promoting the optical qualities of their products while at the same time tending to ignore the simple fact that first and foremost a telescopic sight is a sight — an aiming device — and that we aim with the reticle, not the lenses. The optical qualities and magnification of the scope, whatever they may be, merely support the sight’s only purpose: aiming.

This sounds like a critical assessment, and it is intended to be, because when it comes to reticles, shooters aren’t being led astray so much as they are not being led at all. We get away with this because virtually any reticle, even a bad one, permits pretty good aiming, and as long as the scope can be sighted in and the bullets hit near where we aim on the practice range, we figure that we’re doing OK. What more can be asked?

But shooters and hunters are constantly asking for more, and I have a notion that once they become more acquainted with the relative advantages of different types of reticles, there will be as much campfire debate over crosshairs and dots and posts as there is over the .270 versus the .30-06.

I get a good bit of mail from readers asking for advice when they are planning on buying a new hunting rig. A typical letter reads something like:

“I’m thinking about buying a bolt-action rifle in .280 Remington caliber, and I want to mount a 3X-to-9X variable scope on it. Will this scope be a good all-around choice?”

Very seldom, however, is there an inquiry about the best choice in reticles for different kinds of hunting, even though reticle choice, in many instances, is at least as important as a scope’s magnification, field of view, brightness or any of the other criteria by which a scope is selected.

To get some perspective on the importance of a scope’s reticle, always keep in mind the simple fact that you aim with the reticle. So let’s consider how a reticle affects how you aim.

Read Next: The Best Rifle Scopes for Hunting of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Quite a few years ago, when I first began doing a lot of varmint shooting, I was very much of the opinion that the best reticle was an extremely fine crosshair. My reasoning was that fine crosshairs allowed greater aiming accuracy because very small targets such as thumbtacks, or a woodchuck’s eye, could be divided into precise quadrants. For the most part, this was only wishful thinking because the precise bullet placement that I sought to achieve by such hairsplitting greatly exceeded the accuracy of my rifles and ammunition. Of course, I was also overly optimistic about my marksmanship. To make what I believed to be a good thing even better, I took the crosshairs out of some of my target scopes and replaced them with the thinnest filaments I could find. Youth and innocence require no apology.

More serious, however, was what these slender reticles might have been doing to both my shooting and aiming habits. To aim the fine crosshairs, it was necessary to divide my concentration between the reticle and the target, which, in any shooting situation, is the crooked road to a bad shot. Ideally, the reticle should be of a size and shape that insinuates itself on the target — the image you see in the scope — and transmits the point of aim to your brain without you having to look for it or think about it. That’s why when a reticle is right for the job, you will make a good shot without a clear recollection of having noticed the reticle at all. In other words, the right reticle lets you concentrate on where you want to hit. An apt comparison is a well-fitted shotgun that lets you give your full attention to the flight of the target without having to think about aligning the barrel.

Obviously, what is needed in the way of a reticle is one that is so distinct that it is instantly seen without looking for it and one that remains a distinct element of the sight picture even when you concentrate fully on the target. It would seem then that the ideal reticle would be a broad, very black crosshair, but this is somewhat of an oversimplification because different shapes, as well as sizes, of reticles may be best for different types of shooting.

In recent times, some scope makers have been making a big thing out of the brightness, or “light-gathering” qualities, of their scopes — the idea being that the oversize tubes and objective lenses transmit more light to the shooter’s eye and thereby permit better viewing and aiming during periods of low light, such as at dawn or dusk. This is fine as far as it goes, but without matching the reticle to the hunting conditions, there is little point in having an extra-bright scope.

A while back a scope importer sent me a new model to test that was claimed to be wonderful for shooting in low light. It had a 30mm tube (nearly 3/16 of an inch bigger than a standard one-inch scope tube) and a skillet-size objective (front) lens that transmitted a wonderfully bright field of view. Sadly, though, the scope would have been virtually worthless for hunting in low-light conditions because its standard crosshairs got lost in the evening shadows.

During the many excruciating hours that I’ve spent in a leopard blind, I’ve found over and over that when I’ve had to call it quits on account of darkness, it was not because of being unable to see the target zone, but rather because the reticle in my scope had faded into the gloom. This is why the size and shape of the reticle is more important than the brightness, or so-called “light-gathering” qualities, of a scope that will be used for shooting in dim light.

European hunters, who often shoot in darkness that would astonish their North American counterparts, have long been wise to the absolute necessity of a bold reticle for hunting in poor light. This is why German and Austrian scope makers have traditionally offered not only a wider variety of reticles than American scope makers, but also reticles of much bolder dimensions.

To give you an idea of the difference, the crosswires of a typical 4X American scope will subtend about one-half to three-quarters of a minute of angle at 100 yards. In layman’s terms, this means that the crosswires appear that wide at 100 yards, twice that wide at 200 yards, with progressive enlargements as the range increases. If the reticle is the popular dual-dimension crosshair, such as Leupold’s Duplex pattern, the thicker outer arms of the reticle will subtend about two minutes of angle, more or less.

By comparison, the center wires on a European scope will subtend a full minute of angle, with the thicker arms appearing to be as wide as six to eight inches at 100 yards! Not only that, but the thick arms may reach much closer to the center. These arms reach in so close in some models that even if the thinner center part of the reticle is lost in darkness, the thicker arms can still be used to reasonably aim a shot.

North American hunters, followed by American scope makers, have never cottoned to these bold, extra-thick reticles because they blot out a sizable portion of the field of view, as well as seem to make aiming somewhat imprecise. In truth, though, the broad outer arms of the European reticles don’t block out anything important, and the thick center crosswires, though not the best choice if you want to shoot quarter-inch groups, make it possible to aim a rifle in dim light that would render more delicate reticles useless. My favorite of the European-style reticles has only three heavy arms, with the top arm being omitted. This leaves the top half of the field of view unobstructed, but there is still plenty of reticle definition for aiming in poor light.

I’m not saying that a European-made scope is the only salvation for hunters who take to their deer stands during the darkest minutes of legal shooting hours. There are plenty of scopes made here and in Japan that can be had with low-light reticles. Leupold’s 6×42 scope, for example, comes with a choice of either standard or heavy reticles, with the heavy style having center crosshairs nearly an inch thick (as they appear at 100 yards) and more than 2 1/2 inches wide at the outer arms. Some scope catalogs include tables of reticle subtensions, which I don’t think are often read by consumers but can provide valuable information if you take the time to look at them.

Though the reticles I’ve been discussing may work best in conditions of poor light, there are other hunting and shooting situations where other types of reticles will work better. For example, if you hunt deer in timbered or brushy terrain, where the shooting distance is usually close with the quarry frequently moving or on the run, a heavy European-style crosswire reticle becomes a less than perfect choice. The reason is that when you shoot at a moving target, you want two things: maximum reticle definition and an unobstructed view of the target, especially on the horizontal plain where the target is moving. This latter criterion explains why a reticle with thick horizontal cross arms is a poor choice: As you swing ahead of the running target, the horizontal arms may hide or largely obscure what you are shooting at.

The old-fashioned flat-topped standing-post reticle, with or without visible crosswire, is hard to beat for hunting in brush or timber and for shots at moving game. The bold profile of the post can be easily seen against a brushy background, and the open field of view to either side of the post allows you a clear view of the target even when you are leading a running shot. Troy Lawton, a shooting friend who won the 50-meter running-target event at the U.S. International Shooting Championships a few months ago, tells me that he uses a post reticle for the difficult running-boar events in international competition. Presumably he does this for the reasons that I’ve just described, because what works best in the hunting field frequently works best on the target range as well.

Simple post reticles are not as common in American brands of scopes as they once were. The reason for this, I think, is that modern-day rifle and scope buyers have become overly obsessed with accuracy, and they fear that a post reticle won’t allow the precise aiming that is necessary to shoot bragging-worthy groups at the local club’s range. This is a fundamental but common mistake, because you don’t hunt big game on the practice range. When selecting a hunting reticle, try to imagine how it will look on a miserable, dark, rainy day in heavy brush. In such conditions, a big post can be mighty comforting. That’s why a big post is my first choice in a scope for a shotgun with rifled slugs, because the terrain, hunting conditions and distances at which rifled shotgun slugs are typically used are those where a post reticle is at its best. What with today’s improved slugs and slug-shooting guns, along with hunting regulations requiring their use in some states or regions, I wouldn’t be surprised if the post reticle was to make a comeback. Scope makers take note.

I’ve saved the dot reticle for last because more and more I’ve come to regard a dot as the best all-around reticle for most forms of rifle shooting — especially for any sort of shooting, such as target shooting, plinking and varmint hunting, where careful aiming is required and your eye is kept busy aiming many shots for extended periods. This represents quite a change of opinion, because there was time, long past, when I was of the notion that a dot, no matter how small, covered up too much of the target and thus restricted the accuracy of my aim. But as I mentioned earlier, those were innocent times. Also, a dot reticle nearly caused me a disaster on an Alaska bear hunt several years ago. This I’ll describe presently.

For decades past, the dot reticle has often been referred to as a Lee dot, named after T.K. “Tackhole” Lee, who installed dot reticles in scopes of all types. Lee was famous for his “floating” dot, which was suspended on a filament of spider web so fine as to be all but invisible, making the dot truly appear to float in space. Of course, such dots were a fascinating technical achievement, but in a more practical sense, they left a lot to be desired, as I learned on a cold, drizzly day on the Alaska Peninsula when I tried to draw a bead — or rather a dot — on a bear.

My scope was one of the old 2.5X Lyman Alaskans set in a low Griffin & Howe mount, the way it was done back in the 1950s, and altogether it made for a fine weatherproof rig for hunting bears along the blustery Alaska coast. I’d spotted a nice bear from a hill above and worked my way down to within a range of about 80 yards, remaining hidden in the brush while the brownie scavenged among sea-eroded boulders along the shore. When I raised the .375 Holland & Holland to fire, what I saw was not one dot, but dozens of dots of all sizes, caused by specks of rain on the scope’s eyepiece. By the time I sorted out the dot I wanted to aim with, the bear had disappeared behind a rock and then reappeared several yards down the beach. So I had to make a dash to catch up for another shot, at which point I again played pick the right dot, and the bear once more disappeared. After I had played this guessing game a few more times, the bear stopped long enough for me to get the right dot on target.

Right then I swore off dots, but only for a while. Nowadays I use dot reticles in most of the scopes that I use regularly, especially those that I use for target and varmint shooting, but they aren’t floating dots. Instead, I want the dot suspended on visible wires that instantly lead my eye to the dot. Not only that, but I’ve come to prefer what many shooters would consider oversize dots. The lone exception is the one-eighth of a minute dot in the 36X scope that I use for benchrest shooting. But even such a small dot causes less eye fatigue than crosshairs when a shooter is aiming at a target for long minutes at a time. The same is true with reticles for varmint shooting, only here I prefer a larger dot that can be easily seen against the varied backgrounds typical of varmint-infested pastures.

Where a dot is at its most helpful is in situations where the hunter or target shooter does not have a solid rest and must shoot offhand or from a relatively unsupported position. With the constant twitching of the sights typical of offhand shooting, especially when you’re out of breath or excited about a shot at a trophy deer, ordinary crosshairs can be especially difficult to see as they jiggle and skitter across the target. Trying to keep up with the crosshairs causes you to concentrate on the reticle rather than the target, and as described at the beginning of this column, a miss is in the making.

With a nice plump dot suspended on clearly seen wires, you don’t have to look for or even think about the reticle, and your full attention is focused on where you want the bullet to hit. Also, as you’ll discover, a big dot seems to jiggle less than a crosshair, thus reducing any tendency to jerk the trigger. This is why the dot reticle is an overwhelming favorite with silhouette shooters who fire only from the difficult offhand position. The preferred dot size for silhouette shooting is about a half-minute, which looks big and fat through the high-magnification scopes (16X or more) usually used in competition.

Shooters who use fine crosshairs in the belief that these reticles are an aid to precise aiming (as I thought as a youngster) are only kidding themselves. Savvy shooters, especially experienced target shooters, know that an undersize reticle causes eye fatigue and leads to reduced target concentration. That’s why the top shooters who pump shot after shot into a tiny bull’s-eye use surprisingly large dots or thick crosshairs.

For hunting, the size of the dot should be matched to the magnification of the scope, with lower-power scopes having progressively larger dots. A 4X scope, for example, should have a dot in the 2 1/2 to three-minute range, and a two-minute dot is about perfect for a 6X scope. With modern variable-power scopes, the size of the dot will diminish progressively as the magnification is increased. The dot reticle in Leupold’s 2X-to-7X variable scope, for example, subtends 4.3 minutes of angle at the lower setting and 1.61 minutes at full power, which is ideal.

Whatever reticle you use, be sure that it is perfectly focused for your shooting eye. All too often a scope doesn’t do all it can for a shooter simply because the shooter isn’t seeing the reticle as clearly as he should. Scopes are usually delivered with the eyepiece lens focused for normal vision. But don’t count on the lens being focused, especially when using secondhand scopes. You can easily bring your scope’s reticle into clear focus for your eye by screwing the eyepiece out until the reticle looks fuzzy. Then, while looking through the scope at a neutral background, such as the sky, screw the eyepiece forward (to the right) until the reticle is sharp. While focusing the eyepiece, it is a good idea to look away from the eyepiece every few seconds so that your eye doesn’t accommodate itself to the scope (false focus). Also, if you use prescription glasses when shooting or hunting, be sure to wear them when focusing the eyepiece. Likewise, if you don’t wear your corrective lenses when hunting, focus the scope without them. And if you wear bifocals, be sure to focus the scope while looking through the long-distance part of your glasses.

Remember, the reticle is what you aim with, and the better you see it, the better you’ll shoot.

This story was originally published in the November 1990 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8270. The Appalachian Trail Will Be My 5th Thru-Hike. Here’s What I’m Most Looking Forward To

I’m no stranger to thru-hiking, but I have very little experience with hiking east of the Mississippi River.

Previous hikes of mine have taken me over the spine of the Rocky Mountains on the Continental Divide Trail, through the Sierra Nevada, high up in Washington, and all around the alpine areas of Colorado. Yet I plan to embrace the Appalachian Trail for my next thru-hike and take on all the surprises and unexpected joys that come with exploring a new environment.

It’s hard to prepare for the Appalachian Trail without a sense of pessimism, doom, and gloom about the weather, the terrain, the lack of views, the ticks, and the on-trail crowd permeating all conversations. However, I am actually quite excited for this hike. The same people who tout the discomfort of the AT are often the same people who admit that this trail changed them for the better.

So, as I prepare to embark on five months of terrible weather, aching knees, tree cover, and tick checks, I want to focus on the positives.

The vast majority of my time on trail has been in the remote Western ranges, where towns often sit an hour from trail and fewer people frequent the true backcountry. Finding an unexpected cooler of cold sodas for hikers on trail is virtually unheard of there, and I’m shocked when I hear AT hikers describe the frequency of the support they receive on trail.

I do think there is a particular magic to the support I’ve received on the CDT; there is something to be said for truly unexpected and infrequent acts of kindness from strangers. However, I’m excited to experience what it’s like to get little goodies more often while hiking. Sometimes, those gifts from trail angels hit at the exact moment when you need a morale boost, and I do think the Appalachian Trail is a journey that demands a bit more mental exertion than some others.

When trail magic did happen on the CDT, it was such an unexpected treat. Photo via Katie Jackson

My time hiking out East has been confined to New Hampshire and Vermont’s Long Trail. Out there, not only are the towns close by and frequent, but the towns are also cute.

I have enough friends who live in AT trail towns to know that the culture, food, and community in these towns are truly special. I’m looking forward to revisiting trail towns I love and discovering new ones as I go. In Marion, Virginia, I can’t wait to visit Coach’s gear shop and see the real-life version of the backdrop that so frequently flashes across my social media.

In Hot Springs, I want to soak in mineral water tubs by the river — the CDT turned me into a big believer in a mid-hike hot spring. More than anything, I want to revisit the Dynasty Buffet in Gorham, New Hampshire; I’ve stuffed myself silly there after many hikes in the White Mountains, but I’m excited for the chance to take the all-you-can-eat experience to new heights thanks to true hiker hunger.

Towns along the CDT were so remote that they rarely felt like truly restful stops, especially when you had to almost immediately begin planning how you’d get back to the trail. The Appalachian Trail, I hope, will be a bit more fun in that regard.

I am a big fan of whimsy in a town. Photo via Katie Jackson

Rarely have I heard anyone describe the conditions and terrain of the Appalachian Trail as “forgiving,” but I stand by this phrasing.

I’m sure conditions will be — at times — miserable. Rain, humidity, and heat will wear me down until I’m a shell of a person.

However, from my time on the Long Trail, I know that I rarely feel afraid out East in the way that I sometimes do while hiking out West. Fewer stretches of trail above treeline on the Appalachian Trail means less time I’m hyperfocusing on my fear of lightning. And while the trail is often steep and rocky, it never approaches the level of exposure or technicality that I’ve experienced on trails in Colorado.

Climbing up to this cairn and looking left over the sheer drop is enough to make anyone feel a little wobbly. Also, do not emulate me here when it comes to the bike helmet. That was a terrible decision; if you’re hiking in looser, more technical terrain, just make the investment to get a true helmet. Photo via Katie Jackson

Fear aside, I left the CDT with skin about 50 shades darker and 10 years older than when I started. Even with copious sunscreen application, it’s not a trail that allows you to hide from the sun. On the Appalachian Trail, I expect conditions to be uncomfortable, yes, but also less dangerous and damaging in the long run.

I’m not an expert by any stretch when it comes to botany or fauna, but I do find joy in discovering a wildflower I’ve never seen before or identifying a new bird.

While on the Long Trail, I was shocked by how unfamiliar I was with everything I was passing. I hadn’t thought to download some plant identification apps in advance, so I reached Canada without being able to speak intelligently about the greenery I walked through each day.

On the Appalachian Trail, I’m thrilled for a second chance at this; I want to fully embrace the Green Tunnel and learn to love the massive trees and ferns that embrace the trail. Additionally, I want to find joy in a very different style of wildlife. Things out East tend to be a bit smaller and more understated than what you experience out West; I found this quite meditative during my time on trail in Vermont.

A little newt on the Long Trail. Photo via Katie Jackson

I honestly don’t know if I’ll ever feel the same excitement about spotting a newt as I do for moose or pika, but I am looking forward to developing more of a relationship with the ecology of the East and perhaps even learning to appreciate it just as much.

The sheer contrast of water management out East compared to my other times on trail is something I am genuinely looking forward to. On the CDT, carrying multiple liters and stressing over dry camps on plateaus dictated the rhythm of every single day. Frequently, I had to drink from water sources that were less than ideal.

Knowing that the Appalachian corridor usually has flowing springs every few miles means I can finally enjoy the luxury of mindless hydration. Not only will I no longer need to stay up each night to check the water availability for the following day, but I’ll need to carry far less on my back and will hopefully enjoy much nicer water quality.

If I never need to drink from a muddy cow tank on the Appalachian Trail, I’ll be happy. Photo via Katie Jackson

While hiking out West, you are often moving through landscapes where human presence feels distant, though you do often stumble upon some of the interesting culture of the gold rush and westward expansion. By contrast, the Appalachian Trail passes straight through some of the most history-rich areas of the modern US.

I’ve learned about the Civil War and founding of the country in school, of course, but it will be something else to actually walk through the landscapes where those events played out and learn more specific stories of how that time influenced the area today.

The arts scene in Asheville, NC is vibrant and exciting; I’m excited to walk through a few galleries while smelling terrible. Photo via Katie Jackson

On the Continental Divide Trail, some of my favorite conversations came from locals in towns about their ancestry and history in the area. One of my favorite aspects of thru-hiking is the exposure you get to people you’d never meet in your day-to-day life, and I’m excited for the chance to experience this in an area of the country that is completely new to me.

On the CDT, our tramily joked that when you reached an intersection, the trail probably went down whichever path was less maintained and unmarked. I spent a lot of time backtracking to little turns I missed or bushwhacks I completely bypassed. On the Long Trail, I was shocked by how much mental energy the consistent blazes and well-marked trails saved me.

I understand why the white blazes have become such a beloved symbol of the trail. Being able to keep my phone in my fanny pack and just spot the next white blaze feels so much less stressful than constantly thinking about navigation.

While the trail may seldom be easy, it is often easy to find. Photo via Katie Jackson

All my previous hikes have been NOBO experiences. I’m excited to approach the Appalachian Trail as a southbounder, because I’m sure there are plenty of surprises that come with that. I hope to chase fall colors for at least part of the trail, and while I’m apprehensive about losing daylight, I’ve decided to embrace that and get more experience with night hiking.

Twilight is frequently my favorite time to be hiking anyways. I see more animals during these transition periods and love watching the light dance through the trees. Hopefully, by moving southbound, I’ll dodge some of the crowd while also getting to see a different side of the trail than most.

I’ll get good enough with my nightly routine that I can do it without a headlamp. Photo via Katie Jackson

I am such a lazy hiker. If there is something I can do to make my day easier, I want to do that thing.

On the CDT, I embraced cowboy camping largely to avoid setting up and taking down my tent every night. Out East, I’ll be able to avoid the tent setup as well, but also get a little more protection from the rain by taking advantage of the shelters.

I’m sure that I’ll eventually bemoan the noises and critters that come with shelters, as I so often hear people do, but I am excited for the simplicity and convenience of three walls and a roof over my head.

I also found it easier to pack up in the mornings when I had more dedicated spaces to store my gear overnight. Photo via Katie Jackson

I won’t lie and say I’m expecting to love the Appalachian Trail.

When it comes to the Triple Tiara (the three smaller trails overlapping with the Triple Crown: The Colorado, John Muir, and Long Trails), the Long Trail was my least favorite. Still, I found a beauty and peace in that trail that I hadn’t expected.

I am usually very motivated by the best views, and I just don’t feel that connection to East Coast mountains that allows me to appreciate the sights as much as I appreciate my home mountains out West.

I’m a stubborn person, but I’m not sure I could have finished the CDT if I hadn’t truly loved my day-to-day (in general!). Photo via Katie Jackson

However, you can’t sustainably spend five months on a trail if you don’t have something drawing you in and keeping you there. I’m not sure exactly what it will be about the AT that captivates me.

Maybe it will be the friends I make or the joy of frequent town stops. Maybe I’ll learn to love the Green Tunnel so much that I do truly find it as beautiful as Colorado’s high country. Either way, I will leave this trail with a deeper understanding of the area and, hopefully, a deeper appreciation of it as well.

After thru-hiking the Colorado Trail, John Muir Trail, Continental Divide Trail, and Long Trail in back-to-back years, I'm looking forward to a little time of rest, relaxation, and hanging out with my cat. Or, who knows, maybe the AT. No one has ever accused me of being good at sitting still.

#8268. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8266. Idaho Outfitter Gets Hunting Ban After Illegally Shooting a Trophy Bull in Utah

Published Oct 23, 2026 4:17 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

An eight-year hunting suspension starts this year for an Idaho man who killed a 6×6 bull in Box Elder County, Utah, in 2023. . It’s part of his punishment for hunting Utah elk with a resident license, despite not fulfilling the state’s strict residency requirements.

The Idaho man, whose identity has not been released by the agency, was sentenced for wanton destruction of protected wildlife.

“It is illegal to falsify your residency status when applying for a hunting/fishing license, and may carry severe consequences,” reads the Thursday Facebook post by the Utah DNR Division of Law Enforcement announcing the case’s conclusion.

In the comment section on the DLE’s post about the case, one commenter asked if the Idaho man’s wife would also be charged since she was along for the hunt. Facebook user Lydia Smith replied, in a since-edited comment:

“Everything was legal on that hunt, he just happened to switch his residency because he had just got married, which is what caused all this trouble,” Smith wrote Thursday evening. “So of course Utah hammered him for it and is making it seem like he intentionally poached an animal which isn’t the case. He would have never shot the elk if he knew his tag was forfeit due to residency changes, also why the hell would we post something that was intentionally poached? We have too much to lose to do something stupid like that. This was just an unfortunate situation and he should have looked into the regulations more before hand. But now he knows and is unfortunately paying for it in every way. Also Utah DNR specially doesn’t like him and they’re trying to run his life into the ground. And on an ending note, I wasn’t there when he killed the bull. I showed up afterwards. I also had no idea of the residency issue either. Literally everything was completely legal other than that, which we found out later.”

Smith is a Western hunting guide, artist, and influencer who is married to Sheldon Howe, an Idaho Falls resident and owner of Howe Hunting Company, which operates in Utah, Idaho, and Oregon. Howe could not immediately be reached for comment, but the person who answered the outfit’s phone Friday did not deny Howe’s connection to the case.

The DLE suggested the name of the individual would be redacted in a formal records request, and later declined to confirm or deny Howe’s involvement to Outdoor Life.

The Idaho resident was tasked with paying a $453 fine plus $12,000 in restitution. The court collects the fine while the restitution goes to the state’s Poaching Mitigation Fund. The eight-year hunting suspension not only applies to Utah, it applies to all 50 states through the Interstate Wildlife Violator Compact. It is not immediately apparent how this Utah conviction or the reciprocal hunting ban could affect someone who holds an outfitting license in Idaho or other states.

“We do sometimes see nonresidents obtain licenses. That is something our officers commonly look for to make sure everyone is taking game legally,” Utah Department of Natural Resources Division of Law Enforcement captain Chase Pili tells OL. “The public trusts us to protect resources and follow the rules.”

But in this case, it wasn’t an officer who initially exposed the poach. It was a tipster. The case opened in 2023 after state law enforcement received a tip about a non-resident hunting with a resident license in northern Utah.

“Tips are very important to our agency. This is a perfect example of how we build strong cases from a simple tip from a citizen,” Pili says. “We can never be everywhere at once. We build many cases off tips from the public.”

The state’s law enforcement division receives thousands of tips annually. The captain estimates there’s 385,000 acres to patrol per officer in Utah. Tips help increase eyes on the ground.

“People hunt in droves in certain areas of the state and it helps with prevention when others know not only are officers watching, but the public is watching,” Pili says. “This is a resource that not only we care about, the public cares about as well.”

By the time the illegal license case came together, the elk meat was presumably already eaten, but officers seized the antlers as evidence. The rack will most likely end up becoming a listed item during the state’s periodic poach and roadkill auction.

In a similar case made public in September, Brian Beckstead of Vernal, Utah illegally harvested a 6×6 bull elk while holding resident licenses for Utah and North Dakota at the same time. Investigators also seized that mount. He’s charged with wanton destruction of wildlife.

Read Next: Idaho Made It Much Harder to Get a Lifetime Hunting License After Nonresidents, Influencers Abuse It

This year Idaho made obtaining a lifetime hunting license harder after complaints of nonresidents, including influencers, moving briefly into the state to exploit the lifetime licensing system. The requirement changed from six months of residency to five years. Idaho now has the second-longest requirement of its kind in the country after Wyoming.

#8264. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8262. Week 19 on the CDT

Total elevation gain so far: 121,562m/398,825ft (equivalent of 13.7 Everests)

I’m writing this update from what I expect to be my final resupply town, as we plan the last few sections to take us through to the border with Mexico.

Progress through New Mexico remains swift, with the flatter terrain allowing for big miles each day. The elevation is also dropping, from 8000ft to 5000ft which brings warmer temperatures and more pleasant hiking.

There is one final twist in this journey however, as we have just been notified that the final 2 miles as you approach the border (and terminus monument) is temporarily closed for construction. This means that some alternative options are needed: finish the hike early before reaching the terminus, find an alternative finishing point somewhere else along the border, wait it out until the construction work has finished and the area is reopened. None of these options are ideal, and may extend the hike for another week.

Of all the wildlife I had on my list to see during the CDT, there was one still remaining that was proving elusive – a big cat. These are notoriously rare to see, with both mountain lions and cougars wary of people and hide during the day. For the last couple of days we had seen occasional paw prints in the sand that looked feline, and about 4 inches wide.

The following evening I was hiking late and just after dusk I saw a pair of eyes shining back at me from the bushes. A deer, I thought, as is normal on trail. But instead of darting off, the eyes stayed focussed on me and slowly moving toward me. I could just about make out the outline of its back and shoulders, prowling forward with its head lowered, perfectly still. A cougar. And it was stalking me! Making loud noises and banging my hiking poles together did nothing to deter it, so I backed up along the trail, all the time keeping my headlamp focussed on the eyes shining back at me. It matched my movement step for step, moving silently through the bushes about 30 yards away from me. I continued along the trail, as at least it was no longer advancing towards me, and instead just moving sideways keeping track of me. After a few minutes (which felt much longer) it paused its stalking and just watched me as I put some distance between us. I was doing continuous 360 degree checks for the next few miles!

This was then contrasted by the overly friendly welcome I received at Doc Campbell’s Post, which has 3 young cats (and a very cute dog) to welcome hikers, demand to be fussed over, and try to take some of your food if you leave it unattended for even a second.

Road walks continue to be a feature of this section of the CDT in New Mexico, partly due to the amount of private land, and partly due to having to avoid deep water river crossings. While these are relatively easy and fast, they are also tough on the feet and monotonous. It is hard to stay motivated when you have a 20 or 30 mile walk ahead of you on the same road, which stretches off into the distance.

Over the course of the CDT you meet many hikers time and again, as you cross paths, take different alternates, and have different resupply strategies. I started in Montana in a group of 4, but over the course of time we became separated, only seeing each other occasionally at town stops. During this section however I reconnected with Banshee and BumbleBerry, and is great to be hiking again with them.

The weather has also bunched people up, and it’s been fun to be at a location sheltering from the rain, welcoming them in as they arrive wet and bedraggled, sharing stories of the trail conditions. By the end of the day we had 13 hikers at Doc Campbell’s!

One feature we were all looking forward to was the Gila river, famous for it’s winding path through the valley that it has etched out among the volcanic rock. It features over 200 river crossings along its course, but after recent rains and with more on the way, we chose the safer option and remained on the high route using mainly roads. In some parts, the water crossings were chest deep!

There is also lots of history in this area, with petroglyphs and cave dwellings from the 1200s to explore.

#8261. The Best Shotguns for Bird Hunting of All Time

Published Oct 23, 2026 5:02 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

You could shoot a lifetime of roosters with a beat up Remington 870 Express. And you could make a good argument that any gun you’re willing to carry and can shoot well in the uplands is an upland bird gun.

However, there are some shotguns that are better suited for the task. A good bird hunting gun should be pleasant to carry (meaning it’s light and well balanced), it should mount naturally, and it should swing through targets with ease. A bird gun should look nice too, because as longtime shotgun columnist Phil Bourjaily says, pheasants and grouse don’t like to be killed by ugly guns.

So for this story, and the video above, Bourjaily helped me assemble a list of our favorite bird hunting shotguns, both new and old. We carefully considered value when making our selections. None of the guns on our list are cheap, but they are still attainable for the working bird hunter. They are also the kind of gun that you will want to pass down to your kids one day.

We picked the 12-gauge version of the 825 as our Editor’s Choice award-winning shotgun in 2025, but it’s quite possible that we like the 20 gauge version of the new Citori even better.

Shotgun nerds know that the Browning Citori was introduced in the early 1970s as a more affordable, Japanese-manufactured alternative to John Moses Browning’s Belgian-made Browning Superposed (which you’ll find in our list of classic guns). The modern Citori maintains that legacy of quality and attainability. The Citori 825 has very nice aesthetics. It features a glossy American walnut stock, quail and dove engravings on the receiver, blued barrel, and ivory bead.

With the 28-inch barrels I thought the gun handled perfectly. Even at just 6 pounds, it did not feel whippy at all. Compared to the 725, this upgraded Citori has a lower-profile receiver and lower-bore axis. This should mean less muzzle jump and faster recovery between shots. While shooting this gun on clays, I did notice that it recoiled very lightly.

Lastly, the Citori has a tapered locking bolt that is designed to self-adjust — in other words, tighten — with time. This is meant to prevent a very ambitious shooter from wearing out the action. If you are looking for a do-it-all upland bird gun, it’s hard to beat the Citori in this price range.

The Benelli Montefeltro is probably my all-time favorite pheasant hunting shotgun. It’s light, reliable, and it comes to my shoulder more naturally and quickly than any other semi-auto out there. And sometimes, two shots are just not enough. For Bourjaily’s part, he says that if he had to hunt pheasants for money, this is the gun he would shoot (luckily, or perhaps sadly, that is not the case for Phil).

The Montefeltro was first introduced in 1983, but it was updated most recently in 2023 with an easier-locking bolt system, a two-piece shell latch, and improved ergonomics and grip.

The inertia action in this shotgun allows for a wonderfully sleek and slender shotgun (because there is no need to make room for a gas system in the forend). I like inertia guns best for upland hunting. Typically, you will not be shooting very much, so punishing recoil is not as problematic as it is on a fast and furious duck hunt. Plus you’re less likely to encounter the mud, sand, and dirt that can jam an inertia gun on a waterfowl hunt.

The 20-gauge version of the Montefeltro with a 28-inch barrel weighs only 6.1 pounds. The 12-gauge version at the same barrel length weighs only 6.6 pounds. So take your pick and off to the cattail sloughs you go.

A custom-fitted gun is the ultimate dream for any upland hunter. A gun that has been stocked for you is one you can trust to shoot exactly where you look. The Upland Gun Company Zeus, our  favorite modern side-by-side, is made one at a time, to each individual shooter’s specifications. You get to choose your stock dimensions, chokes, barrel length and wood. And you are able to do so at a price that’s not that far out of line with a good production double.

The guns are made by RFM, a small Italian maker, and imported by the Upland Gun Company, co-founded by Jerry Havel and Dan LaFond who once competed with each other in the Upper Midwest shotgun scene. Havel was a Remington rep and LaFond repped Mossberg. After years as rivals, they founded a company that made the side-by-side guns they both loved.

If you would like to own one of these guns, but don’t know your dimensions, you schedule a fitting with Upland Gun Company, which is based in Remer, Minnesota. Then you choose your options. Some options are free, some are upcharges — like higher-grade wood, double triggers, extra choke tubes, case color or blued frame. Then you wait for nine months to a year while RFM makes your gun.

For Bourjaily’s shotgun, he chose 30-inch barrels and fixed chokes, upgraded wood, case color, a straight grip, and a slight beavertail forend.

What you get with the Upland Gun Company is a gun that is yours, that fits you, and is truly one-of-a-kind. If you pick too many extras your gun can cost a lot but if you keep yourself under control, you get a custom gun at almost off-the-rack pricing, and that is worth the wait.

This is an incredibly light shotgun. The 12-gauge version I have weighs only 6.4 pounds. Beretta achieved this weight saving by modifying and skeletonizing its 690 action and using plastic inserts. To my eye the gun still looks great, despite the plastic. Beretta removed wood from the stock, selected a thin recoil pad, and skipped the side ribs between the barrels. Minimalist and non-traditional would be accurate descriptors for this shotgun.

This 20-gauge over/under has a history as an affordable, American-made shotgun for the blue-collar bird hunter. This resurrected version of the gun is made for Ruger by Connecticut Shotgun Manufacturing Company. If you are not familiar with that brand, CSMC is known for building fine, high-end shotguns in, you guessed it, Connecticut. And while the Red Label III is pricier than Bill Ruger’s original vision, it’s safe to say that it’s much nicer, too. Read my full review of the Red Label III here.

This Dickinson was our pick for the best affordable side-by-side. The Plantation is full of nice features, including the bone and charcoal finish, plus clean checkering that is as functional as it is good looking. The Plantation has snappy ejectors that send hulls flying with authority. In the field, the gun was easy to carry and came to the shoulder quickly. Everyone who shot it agreed the balance was ideal, and they liked the gun’s rib and brass bead.

We reviewed the 28-gauge, 3-inch version of this gun and found it to be handy and light recoiling. The gun was a joy to shoot. The 28-inch barrel swung to targets well and the shotgun mounted quickly. With target loads, recoil was incredibly minimal and even with 3-inch game loads the gun was mild shooting. While it was fun testing the 28-gauge version, I would recommend getting this gun in 20 gauge for maximum versatility.

The Auto 5 was a marvel in its day. It was the first successful mass-produced semi-auto shotgun and it was made in Belgium starting in 1902. The Auto 5 utilizes a long-recoil system, in which both the bolt and the barrel move to the rear to re-cock the hammer after a shell is fired. Then the barrel moves forward, the bolt follows and chambers the next shell from the magazine. Friction rings on the magazine tube were designed to allow the firing of light and heavy loads, which was a major hurdle at the time.

The 16-gauge version of this shotgun, aptly named the “Sweet 16,” was introduced in 1936. Browning lightened the gun by removing steel from the barrel ring and receiver and wood from the stock. The promise was a semi-auto shotgun that carried like a 20 gauge and hit like a 12 gauge. And on this promise, Browning delivered.

Today, 16-gauge shotguns are not quite as appealing, since modern 20 gauges can fire 3-inch shells delivering just as much payload in an even lighter platform. But our love for this gun is more about nostalgia than practicality. As Bourjaily wrote for us in his full review of the gun: “No other shotgun feels quite like an original Browning Auto 5 when it goes off. The entire barrel moves backward with the bolt, then forward as it picks up the next shell and returns to battery. That unique bouncing recoil sensation, the Auto 5’s many fans will tell you, is just one more way you know that you’re shooting the greatest semi-auto shotgun ever made.”

In the field, I shot this gun quite well. It came to the shoulder naturally and crushed clays and roosters alike. Unlike some old guns, it did not feel bulky or clunky at all. Loading a third shell into the magazine was a bit of a challenge, but perhaps back in the day, men had tougher thumbs and more resolve. In any case, after shooting this gun (which belongs to OL executive editor Natalie Krebs) I’ve been shopping for one of my own on the used market, where there are options ranging from about a grand to well over $2,000.

As Bourjaily writes, before the Browning Superposed, over/unders were handmade, bespoke sidelock shotguns priced far out of reach of the average person. John Browning saw the O/U and realized that American shooters, who were accustomed to looking down the single barrel of a pump or semi-auto, would like what he called the single sighting plane of an O/U shotgun. He set out to make an O/U that an average person could afford if they saved for it. Browning wanted to make an aspirational gun. He designed it to be simpler than an English gun, to be made with some mass-produced parts and he worked with FN in Belgium, as he did with many other guns.

Browning’s work on the Superposed began in the 1920s, when the economy was strong, skeet shooting was a fad, and there was a wide variety of game to hunt.

Browning died in 1926, literally while at work on the gun. His son Val finished it, but the Superposed was born into a global depression, then a world war that resulted in the occupation, then the destruction, of the factory where it was being built. In the 1950s, the Superposed became the gun that Browning always thought it would be, until the 70s when high cost of Belgian labor forced Browning to move production to Japan and simplify the design into the Citori, which is largely the same gun.

The Superposed is more than an artifact of shotgunning history. In its Lightning and Superlight configurations, John Browning’s O/U still makes a great upland bird gun as it nears its 100th birthday. The heavier 3-inch magnum guns have to be babied with bismuth, but they can drop ducks and pheasants as well as any modern gun. In any configuration, the Superposed is durable, reliable, well-made and good-looking. The 20-gauge version is especially well-suited for carrying in the uplands.

The Ruger Gold Label might not be everybody’s pick for the top classic side-by-side, but we have our reasons. The Gold Label was one of Bill Ruger’s last guns and it was only made for a short time. This gun might be the last classic American double.

All of the Foxes and Parkers and Ithacas became casualties of WWII. They became too expensive to produce, and no one wanted them in postwar America. Fifty years later, Ruger aimed to make an affordable, high quality side by side for American hunters, and the Gold Label was the result.

His design was inspired by Scottish round actions, in which all the parts of the lock sit on the trigger plate so the receiver can be rounded and petite.

Ruger guns were made with investment casting rather than machining to reduce costs.

Bill intended this gun to sell for $2,000 in 2004, which would be about $3,500 today. And that is about what these guns sell for on the used market. Unfortunately, Ruger had a hard time manufacturing the Gold Label under that price point and ultimately the guns lost money.

The Gold Label was introduced as a svelte 12 gauge that weighs only 6.5 pounds. Since the frame is so light, the gun has a very weight-forward balance, which makes it easy to shoot.

We shot Bourjaily’s Gold Label and he admits that he doesn’t love the stainless frame, but he does love the lines of the round action, which we agree are the most beautiful shotguns ever made. We can’t afford the great Scottish round actions — like a MacNaughton or a David McKay Brown — but we can afford this gun, and so can you if you really want one. Ruger eventually gave up Bill’s pet project after he died. There were only 3,000 Gold Labels made, which leaves 2,999 out there for you to find.

Read Next: Best Shotguns, Tested and Reviewed

Our roster of shotguns represents the middle ground of upland bird guns. Of course there are much more expensive over/unders and side-by-sides out there that will turn heads at any hunt club. There are also a bunch of cheap Turkish-made guns that will drop birds for you without fuss.

But the guns on our list will get the job done with a little more style and reliability. They are not so nice that you’ll feel bad about putting a scratch or two in the stock. In other words, they are hard working shotguns that are easy to carry, shoot, and they look good while doing it.

#8259. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8257. Where to Shoot a Deer: Everything Hunters Need to Know About Shot Placement

Published Oct 24, 2026 8:34 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Knowing where to shoot a deer for a quick kill is the responsibility of every deer hunter. Most of us were taught that the best place to shoot a deer is the “boiler room,” which means the top of the heart and the lungs. For the vast majority of hunting scenarios, that’s still the best option. Penetrating these vital organs (with a bullet or an arrow) leads to massive blood loss and a quick death. It also results in very minimal meat damage.

So, if you know you want to shoot a deer in the heart and lungs, where exactly should you aim?

Put simply, if the deer is broadside, follow the front leg up the deer and aim just below the halfway point on its chest. Look for the “crease” that the deer’s shoulder creates. Shooting with a rifle, you can edge tighter to the deer’s shoulder. Bowhunters want to hit just an inch or two behind the crease, which allows a little more room for error (more on this later).

There isn’t much of a difference in aim point for rifle hunters or bowhunters, as you can see in the photo below.

The video below, created by the National Deer Association, does an excellent job explaining where to shoot a deer on an anatomically correct deer target. Look closely at the bone structure of a deer’s shoulder. It is not one solid mass of bone. First the bone angles forward of the leg and then the shoulder blade sweeps back. Understanding this anatomy is especially important for archers who generally want to avoid hitting these large bones with their arrow (well constructed rifle bullets will easily blast through bones). This is a key difference for bowhunters: There’s simply a much smaller margin of error.

Now, the discussion on where to shoot a deer gets more complicated when deer are quartering away from you or angling toward you. You still want to hit the vital area of the heart and lungs, but now you must change your aim point. The best way to do this is to visualize where the heart and lungs are placed within the deer’s body cavity and aim so that your bullet or arrow angles through them. In general, this means holding farther back on quartering away shots and farther forward on quartering-to shots.

Many hunters prefer quartering-away shots to broadside shots. In some cases, the angle creates a larger margin of error for hitting the lungs. Plus, the deer is facing away from you so it’s easier to draw or shoulder your gun without being detected.

Visualize an angle that takes your bullet or arrow through the deer’s heart and lungs and then continues into its offside shoulder, or just in front of it. One way to do this is to look at the offside leg. Follow the front of the offside leg up to the body.

The photo above is the aim point for bowhunters on this angle. Rifle hunters should aim a few inches farther forward.

Quartering-to shots are not ideal for bowhunters. This is because you must hold into the shoulder or risk hitting guts. Lighter arrows and lower draw weight bows will not penetrate bones in the deer’s shoulder. But for rifle hunters shooting quality bullets, the quartering-to angle still presents a good shot opportunity. You must hold into the frontside shoulder now, with your bullet exiting the middle or back of the rib cage. This shot will damage more meat than a well-executed broadside shot.

Frontal shots can be incredibly effective but they offer a smaller margin of error than broadside shots. When a deer is facing directly toward you, aim between the two shoulders, just below the half-way point on its chest. Executed properly, this shot typically drops deer very quickly. Because your target is much narrower at this angle, however, this shot should only be taken at close ranges.

Bowhunters who hunt from the ground and rattle in or decoy bucks commonly see frontal shots. If you’re a bowhunter and intend to take frontal shots, you should opt for a heavy arrow with a high FOC and heavy, durable fixed-blade broadheads. But most importantly, you must have your setup tuned properly and be able to shoot baseball sized groups without fail.

You will see some hunters bragging online about the “Texas heart shot” which means shooting a deer that is facing straight-away, through the anus. It’s true that when this shot is made properly, with a rifle, it can be quickly fatal. The bullet passes through the rear end of the deer and takes out its vitals in front. Essentially, it’s the same as the frontal shot but in reverse.

However hunters (and especially bowhunters) should pass on this shot angle. Deer are often angling away, not walking perfectly straight away. So it’s very likely that you’ll hit the deer in the ham and miss the vital organs. Also, a deer presenting this shot angle is likely moving, which only increases the likelihood of a marginal hit. The one exception here is when making a followup shot. If you know you hit the deer with your first shot (and are unsure of how well) then it’s wise to follow up with a going-away shot if you can.

Shooting a deer with a bow is more complicated than shooting one with a gun. As we’ve already discussed, there’s less margin for error with archery gear. Plus, since bowhunters are often hunting from treestands and taking close-range shots, they have to account for the sharper angle of the shot. Lastly, deer commonly jump a bow string on farther shots, meaning they duck or spin the instant you loose your arrow. In many cases, bowhunters should aim slightly lower on their target, even if they intend to hit a deer in the heart/lungs. Here’s what you need to know about where to shoot a deer with a bow.

Many bowhunters advocate for shooting deer through the shoulder in the “vital V,” instead of the crease. By this they mean, holding into the deer’s shoulder, where its humerus and scapula make a sideways V shape. If you place your arrow through this window, it’s unarguably deadly. There are no bones (besides the ribcage) in this V. Plus, bowhunters shooting heavy arrows, stout draw weights, and durable fixed-blade broadheads are able to penetrate these bones without issue anyway. The YouTube personality “Ranch Fairy” has been one of the most prominent modern advocates of aiming for the Vital V, and you can see his explanation in the video below.

Aiming for the vital V is problematic, however, especially for new bowhunters. If you pull your shot low or forward, you’ll hit heavy bones in the shoulder, which your arrow might not pass through. Plus, the lungs narrow in the deer’s forward body cavity. Most bowhunter’s education courses, and this author recommend holding farther back into the crease of the deer’s shoulder, and not aiming for the vital V.

As long as you’re using quality archery gear, a well-placed shot through the crease will be deadly, almost without fail. Arrow weight, broadhead style, and draw weight aren’t as much of a factor here. Plus, you have slightly more room for error by holding behind the shoulder. By aiming for the crease, you’re holding for the area on the deer’s body where the lungs are the tallest and widest. If you miss a little forward, you’ll likely hit the vital V, if you miss a little back, you’ll likely hit the back of the lungs and liver.

It’s also easy to see the crease and use it as a specific spot to aim for. Picking a singular aim point is crucial.

Read Next: Why Mechanical Broadheads Are Still the Best Option for Most Deer Hunters

When shooting from a tree stand, your arrow will be striking deer at a downward angle. The higher your stand and the closer the deer, the steeper this angle will be. For example, if you’re 20 feet up, shooting a deer that’s 15 yards away, you’ll be shooting downward at an approximately 60-degree angle. When your arrow strikes the deer, it will look something like the photo below.

So for close shots at a steep angle, you want to aim slightly higher. This ensures your arrow will pass through both lungs. But the keyword here is “slightly.” Generally speaking, hitting a deer too high with a bow is bad.

The best thing you can do to master elevated shot angles to is practice them. Use  a 3D target and shoot from an elevated position, as if you were in a treestand. This will help you get an instinctual understanding of where to hold for different shot angles. You want your arrow to pass through the top of the near lung and the bottom of the far lung.

All of this gets a bit more difficult for bowhunters because so often deer jump the string or duck at the sound of the bow releasing. This is typically only an issue beyond 20 yards. Some bowhunters solve for this by simply aiming a little lower for farther shots. For shots beyond 20 yards, it’s a good idea to hold a little lower, but still in the vital zone. However there is no rule or formula for outsmarting string-jumping deer.

“Their reactions are so dynamic and different in every situation that you cannot predict what the deer is going to do,” says Aaron Warbritton of The Hunting Public. “Over all the video we’ve watched, we noticed that some deer would duck straight down to the ground. Some deer would drop a foot at 30 yards. Others would drop four inches at 30 yards. Still other deer would not move at 30 yards. Some would duck and roll away. So, they would be broadside at 30 yards, duck six inches, roll away and by the time the arrow impacted, the deer is actually quartering away instead of broadside.”

Every scenario is slightly different, but here are some basic tips and takeaways to deal with deer jumping the string:

Because rifle bullets carry so much more energy and generally do more damage to bones and organs, rifle hunters have more options besides the heart and lung area. With a heart/lung-shot, deer often run off even though they die quickly. A heart-shot deer can still make it 100 yards. Some hunters want to drop deer in their tracks, so should these hunters aim elsewhere? We asked a number of deer cullers—sharpshooters whose job requires them to kill deer quickly, for their perspectives on bullet placement. Their advice, detailed below, is: “It depends” on distance, bullet type, shooting ability, and your goals for meat retention. Besides the heart and lung area, other options include high-shoulder, neck, and head. There are pros and (major) cons to each.

Pros: The ultimate shock-and-awe shot. A big, fast-moving bullet will likely snap the spine, short-circuit the nervous system, break bones, and anchor a deer where it stands.

Cons: The volatile, upsetting bullets best suited for this shot damage a lot of meat, from the shoulder through the neck and upper backstrap. Plus, it’s easy to miss high when aiming here.

When you sharpshoot deer for a living, as Grant Woods did for 21 years, “you can’t afford misses or wounded deer running around,” he says. Both cost you time and money—especially a wounded, bleeding deer, running for its life and spooking other deer.

Woods, a noted whitetail biologist, did much of his deer-­control work on golf courses. There, shots usually ranged between 200 and 300 yards. His first choice was the double-shoulder shot, with a .308 round entering a shoulder blade on one side, slamming through the body and into the far shoulder blade.

“If you watch slow-motion video of a deer being shot this way, its whole body flexes when the bullet hits,” says Woods. “That snaps the spine. That deer’s never going to move again.” This shot can damage more meat than the heart-lung approach, but the benefit is that the deer will likely drop immediately.

Pros: A deer dies instantly when its brain takes a direct hit. Plus, there is very little meat lost to a head shot.

Cons: The brain is a tiny target, and it’s easy to miss the deer entirely or, worse, to wound it through the jaw.

How do you guarantee a drop-it-where-it-stands shot? For Anthony DeNicola, owner of White Buffalo, a top deer-control operation, it’s all about the brain.

“Draw a line from tear duct to tear duct, then go 2.5 to 2.75 inches above that line, centered,” says DeNicola. “That’s where you want to place your bullet—first and best option.”

A bullet in the brain instantly incapacitates the animal; death follows in seconds. Of course, DeNicola and his team have an advantage over hunters: They shoot at night with infrared optics, from raised mobile platforms, over bait, at known distances (usually 50 to 60 yards), and (where legal) with suppressed rifles.

DeNicola uses .223-caliber rifles, firing 50- to 55-grain frangible varmint projectiles that expend all their energy into the brainpan. In the urban and suburban environments in which he works, DeNicola can’t afford to have a round exiting an animal.

The second best shot placement for headshots is a brain shot from the side. DeNicola’s third choice is a shot just below the back of the skull in the first four cervical vertebrae of the spine.

“The deer drop immediately,” DeNicola says of the vertebrae shot. “Heart and lung functions will cease. They lose consciousness and die in eight to 12 seconds.”

For hunters, however, taking head shots is ill-advised.

“There’s simply no margin for error around a deer’s relatively small brain (about 3 inches on the average deer, as much as 4 inches on a large adult buck),” NDA’s Lindsay Thomas wrote for OL earlier this year in his column, Don’t Aim for a Deer’s Head. “Plus, a deer’s brain is a deceptively small target. Yes, a big whitetail might look like it has a large head. But for reference, compare a deer shoulder mount to a skull mount. With the skull mount, you’ll see that the cranial cavity only makes up a small portion of the skull. It would be easy for hunters to misjudge the location of the brain, within the skull, on a live, moving deer.”

Head shots should be reserved for sharpshooters only.

Pros: A correctly placed bullet will kill with massive shock to the spinal cord and vertebrae while damaging very little meat.

Cons: The vital area on a neck shot is quite small. Hit low, and you will wound a deer with very little chance of recovery. Plus, this shot often merely paralyzes a deer, requiring a second shot.

Like the head shot, the neck is a deceptively small target. This is especially true for bucks with swollen necks during the rut. Unless the deer is at close range and you are extremely confident in your marksmanship, avoid attempting neck shots and wait for a better opportunity.

The best shot on a deer is tight behind the shoulder, through the lungs and heart.

Deer can survive a shoulder shot if the projectile doesn’t penetrate through the scapula or humerus bones. Deer that are hit high behind the shoulder often survive, too.

At the risk of sounding like a broken record, shooting a deer tight behind the shoulder, through the lungs and heart, is ideal placement, and does not ruin meat.

Unless you’re a professional sharp shooter, the old school deer hunters had it right all along on where to shoot a deer. The best shot placement for deer is through the lungs and the top of the heart, just behind the shoulder. With any standard deer hunting cartridge or any quality broadhead, a well-executed shot here will mean a quick death for the deer, plus a highly visible and short blood trail for the hunter to follow. Study whitetail anatomy before heading to the woods. And when you see deer while hunting, pay close attention to their body angles and the resulting shot presentations. It’s good practice to visualize your aim point on real live deer, even when your not intending to harvest that particular animal. That way when it is time to shoot, you’ll know exactly where.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.
